A.io: Non-ST segment elevation
A.q: A 64-year-old man with a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction is stabilized and taken to the catheterization laboratory. Dye shows a tight narrowing of the anterior interventricular artery, which is opened with a balloon and held open with a drug-eluting stent. Which term names the procedure that opened the artery?
opts: Plain old balloon angioplasty
Plain old balloon angioplasty opens a narrowed artery without a stent. Once a stent is left in place to hold the artery open, the procedure is a percutaneous coronary intervention.
Left heart catheterization
Left heart catheterization is the introduction of a guidewire for access to the heart chambers and coronary arteries. It is the access, not the stent that opened the vessel.
Percutaneous coronary intervention

Correct. Percutaneous coronary intervention is the placement of a drug-eluting or non-drug-eluting stent to keep the coronary artery open. Anything done to the vessel during the catheterization, beyond imaging it, is the intervention.
Coronary angiography
Coronary angiography is the injection of dye to identify the lesion or blockage. It showed the narrowing here, but it did not open the artery; the stent placement did.

A.q: What is the normal relationship between leg and arm systolic pressure?
opts: The relationship varies unpredictably and cannot be used
The relationship is consistent enough to be diagnostically useful when coarctation is suspected.
They are normally identical
Leg systolic normally exceeds arm systolic rather than matching it, which is what makes a leg pressure equal to or below the arm a meaningful finding.
Arm systolic is normally higher than leg
The normal relationship runs the other way, which is what makes a reversal meaningful in suspected coarctation.
Leg systolic is normally higher than arm
Correct, so a leg pressure that is not higher is the abnormal finding. Leg pressures are measured when the pulse examination suggests coarctation.

A.q: How does the body respond to increased metabolic demand in heart failure?
opts: Slows heart rate to lengthen filling time
The response is the opposite: neurohormonal input increases heart rate, alongside greater contractility and augmented preload.
Lowers contractility to spare oxygen
Contractility rises through catecholamines and autonomic input, together with heart rate and preload.
Raises heart rate, contractility and preload

Correct. Neurohormonal input raises the heart rate, catecholamines and autonomic input raise contractility, and venous capacitance and renal compensation augment preload. These help at first and later drive damage.
Lowers preload through venous pooling
Preload is augmented, not lowered, through venous capacitance and renal compensation, alongside a faster heart rate and greater contractility.

A.io: Mitral valve prolapse
A.q: A 24-year-old woman has a mid-systolic click at the apex. An echocardiogram is ordered. Which finding confirms the suspected valve problem?
opts: A dilated tricuspid annulus
A dilated tricuspid annulus causes tricuspid regurgitation in pulmonary hypertension. The echo finding of prolapse is thickened, redundant mitral leaflets.
A dilated aortic root
A dilated aortic root is a cause of aortic regurgitation found on echo. Prolapse is confirmed by thickened, redundant mitral leaflets over 5 mm.
Thick, redundant mitral leaflets

Correct. Mitral valve prolapse is diagnosed by echocardiogram showing thickened, redundant mitral leaflets greater than 5 mm, flaring into the left atrium during systole, from myxomatous degeneration.
A calcified, narrowed aortic valve
Thickened, calcified aortic leaflets with reduced opening are the echo finding of aortic stenosis. Prolapse shows thickened, redundant mitral leaflets.

A.io: Tricuspid stenosis
A.q: A 49-year-old woman with severe tricuspid stenosis develops worsening hepatic congestion, and her team fears progression to cirrhosis. Which intervention is reserved for this situation?
opts: Afterload reduction therapy only
Afterload reduction treats chronic aortic regurgitation. Tricuspid stenosis threatening cirrhosis calls for balloon valvotomy or valve repair.
Mitral valve clip placement
A mitral valve clip treats severe mitral regurgitation. Hepatic congestion from tricuspid stenosis is the indication for balloon valvotomy or repair.
Transcatheter aortic valve replacement
Transcatheter aortic valve replacement treats severe aortic stenosis. In tricuspid stenosis with threatening hepatic congestion, balloon valvotomy or repair is reserved.
Balloon valvotomy or valve repair
Correct. Balloon valvotomy and valve repair are reserved for tricuspid stenosis with hepatic congestion that may lead to cirrhosis, or with severe systemic venous congestion.

A.q: A 45-year-old man has two days of breathlessness after a viral illness. His N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide is 90. How should the result be read?
opts: The result is indeterminate
At 90 the result is clearly below the rule-out level of 300. Acute heart failure is ruled out.
Heart failure is likely
Younger than 75, heart failure becomes likely above 125. A level of 90 rules out acute failure.
Acute heart failure is likely
Nothing near this level suggests acute failure. Below 300 the N-terminal fragment rules it out.
Acute heart failure is ruled out
Correct. An N-terminal fragment below 300 rules out acute heart failure with a negative predictive value above 90%, and 90 is also below the under-75 heart failure threshold of 125.

A.q: An 80-year-old man in the intensive care unit with acute heart failure has cool extremities and hypotension, and inotropic support is being considered. Which agents are used for this?
opts: Dobutamine or milrinone
Correct. Inotropic therapy for intensive care use includes the sympathomimetics dobutamine, norepinephrine and epinephrine and the phosphodiesterase inhibitor milrinone.
Spironolactone or eplerenone
These are mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists for chronic reduced ejection fraction. Inotropic support uses dobutamine or milrinone.
Diltiazem or verapamil
These are calcium channel blockers, which are avoided in heart failure. Inotropic support uses dobutamine or milrinone.
Losartan or irbesartan
These are angiotensin receptor blockers for chronic therapy. Inotropic support in intensive care uses dobutamine or milrinone.

A.q: How is droxidopa usually used?
opts: As sole first-line therapy for fainting
First-line care is removing the cause or trigger and slow position changes; droxidopa is a mild adjunct rather than a first-line agent.
As an emergency infusion in intensive care
The emergency and intensive care drugs are epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine, phenylephrine and vasopressin.
As an adjunct to midodrine or fludrocortisone
Correct. Droxidopa has only mild efficacy, so it is usually added to midodrine or fludrocortisone, and it is the better choice when supine hypertension is present.
As a substitute for trigger avoidance
Reflex syncope is managed by trigger avoidance and safety precautions, which a drug does not replace.

A.q: A 68-year-old smoker with peripheral arterial disease has blood pressure of 168/94 despite three agents. An abdominal bruit is audible, ultrasound shows a right kidney 2 cm smaller than the left, and he has had two episodes of sudden pulmonary edema. What is the most likely underlying cause?
opts: Obstructive sleep apnea
Sleep apnea contributes to resistant hypertension, but through nocturnal sympathetic activation, without bruits or asymmetric kidneys.
Chronic kidney disease from diabetes
Diabetic kidney disease reduces both kidneys' function together rather than producing a 2 cm size discrepancy with a bruit.
Renovascular disease

Correct. The cluster is characteristic: resistant pressure, an abdominal bruit, asymmetric kidneys and recurrent flash pulmonary edema. In an older patient with established vascular disease the mechanism is atherosclerotic stenosis, often bilateral and progressive.
Primary aldosteronism
Aldosteronism also presents with resistant hypertension, but with unexplained hypokalemia rather than asymmetric kidneys and an abdominal bruit.

A.q: A 3-year-old boy is brought for a routine visit. His father had a heart attack at 40 and was found to have very high cholesterol. What is the most appropriate step regarding the boy's lipids?
opts: Elective lipid screening now
Correct. Elective screening is appropriate for patients as young as 2 years old with a family history of heart disease or high cholesterol.
Start a statin without testing
A statin follows a diagnosis of familial hypercholesterolemia; he has not yet been tested.
Wait until age 9 to 11
Routine screening is at 9 to 11, but his father's premature disease and high cholesterol justify elective screening now.
Screen only after puberty
His father's premature heart attack and high cholesterol make screening appropriate from age 2, well before puberty.

A.q: A 16-year-old girl has palpitations and dizziness on standing. Within 10 minutes of standing her heart rate rises from 70 to 114, and her pressure does not fall. Does this meet the heart rate criterion for her age?
opts: Yes; any rise over 20 per minute
A rise of 20 is too low for any age group; the adult threshold is more than 30 and the adolescent threshold 40.
No; adolescents need a rise of 50
The adolescent threshold is 40 beats per minute, and her rise of 44 clearly exceeds it.
No; the rise must occur in 3 minutes
The window for this syndrome is 10 minutes; 3 minutes is the window for orthostatic pressure criteria.
Yes; the rise exceeds 40 per minute
Correct. In adolescents the threshold is an increase of 40 beats per minute; her rise of 44 within 10 minutes meets it.

A.q: A 53-year-old man on an angiotensin receptor blocker and a dihydropyridine remains above goal at maximally tolerated doses. What is the next step?
opts: Add an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor
Dual renin-angiotensin blockade is prohibited because of hyperkalemia and kidney injury risk.
Add spironolactone now
Spironolactone is the fourth agent, added only after the foundational three have been optimized.
Add a thiazide-type diuretic

Correct. The foundational three are a renin-angiotensin blocker, a dihydropyridine and a thiazide-type diuretic, all titrated before resistance can be considered confirmed. It is the third of the foundational agents.
Add a second dihydropyridine
Duplicating a class adds adverse effects without the complementary mechanism a third class gives.

A.io: Compare and contrast precipitating factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis (including role of B-type natriuretic peptide, BNP), and treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
A.q: A 69-year-old woman has sudden severe breathlessness, crackles and edema. Her B-type natriuretic peptide is 1,150. How should this level be read?
opts: Only chronic heart failure fits
Levels above 900 point to acute heart failure, and her sudden onset fits. The result makes acute failure likely.
The result is indeterminate
The indeterminate range is 100 to 400. A level of 1,150 makes acute heart failure likely.
Acute heart failure is likely
Correct. Above 900 acute heart failure is likely. Above 400 heart failure is likely in general, 100 to 400 is indeterminate, and below 100 rules acute failure out.
Acute heart failure is ruled out
Rule-out applies only below 100. A level of 1,150 is far above that and makes acute heart failure likely.

A.io: Differentiate each stage of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA), natural history classification of heart failure, and associated treatment recommendations of each stage.
A.q: A 60-year-old man with hypertension has never had cardiac symptoms. An echocardiogram shows left ventricular hypertrophy with preserved function. Which heart failure stage is he in?
opts: Stage A
Stage A is risk factors with a normal heart. Hypertrophy is structural disease, which puts him in stage B even without symptoms.
Stage B
Correct. Asymptomatic structural heart disease, including left ventricular hypertrophy, is stage B, pre-heart failure. Stage A requires a structurally normal heart.
Stage C
Stage C requires past or current symptoms. He has never had any, so his hypertrophy places him in stage B.
Stage D
Stage D is advanced heart failure. Asymptomatic hypertrophy is stage B, pre-heart failure.

A.q: Which diastolic change on standing meets the orthostatic criterion?
opts: A fall of more than 10 mmHg within 10 minutes
The window for orthostatic pressure criteria is 3 minutes; the 10-minute window belongs to the tachycardia syndrome's heart rate criteria.
A fall of more than 30 mmHg within 3 minutes
More than 30 mmHg is the systolic threshold used when baseline pressure is elevated with supine hypertension, not the diastolic criterion.
A fall of more than 20 mmHg within 3 minutes
More than 20 mmHg within 3 minutes is the systolic threshold with a normal baseline, not the diastolic one.
A fall of more than 10 mmHg within 3 minutes
Correct. A diastolic fall of more than 10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing meets the orthostatic criterion alongside the systolic thresholds.

A.q: A 44-year-old man with episodic headache, sweating, palpitations and pallor has raised plasma free metanephrines and an adrenal mass. He is scheduled for resection. What must be established before surgery?
opts: Alpha blockade first, then beta blockade
Correct, and the order is not negotiable: isolated beta blockade leaves alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed and can precipitate a hypertensive crisis.
Neither, provided the tumor is resected promptly
Blockade is required before resection to prevent catecholamine surge during manipulation.
Beta blockade first, then alpha blockade
This reversal is the dangerous one. Beta blockade without prior alpha blockade leaves vasoconstriction unopposed.
Either order, provided both are established before surgery
The sequence itself matters, which is why alpha blockade is specified first and beta blockade only afterwards.

A.io: Tricuspid regurgitation
A.q: A 71-year-old woman with long-standing pulmonary hypertension and a dilated right ventricle develops a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that increases with inspiration. Which process most likely produced her valve leak?
opts: Endocarditis of the leaflets
Infective endocarditis is the primary cause of tricuspid regurgitation in injection drug users. With pulmonary hypertension and a dilated ventricle, annular dilation is the cause.
Dilation of the tricuspid annulus
Correct. The most common cause of tricuspid regurgitation is dilation of the tricuspid annulus from right ventricular dilation in the setting of pulmonary hypertension.
Rheumatic leaflet narrowing
Rheumatic disease narrows valves, most commonly the mitral, causing stenosis. Her leak is from annular dilation due to right ventricular dilation.
A prior valvuloplasty
A prior valvuloplasty for outflow obstruction is the most common cause of significant pulmonic regurgitation. Her tricuspid leak comes from annular dilation.

A.q: A 70-year-old man with heart failure and congestion is started on furosemide. Which counseling point is most appropriate?
opts: No blood tests are needed on this drug
Monitoring is needed. Furosemide wastes potassium, so potassium and renal function are followed on the metabolic panel.
It will raise his potassium to high levels
Loop diuretics waste potassium rather than raising it; it is the mineralocorticoid antagonists that spare it. Potassium and renal function will be checked.
His liver enzymes will be checked weekly
Liver tests are not the monitoring a loop diuretic needs. Potassium and renal function are followed on the metabolic panel.
Potassium and kidney labs will be checked
Correct. Furosemide is a potassium-wasting loop diuretic, so potassium and renal function are followed on the complete metabolic panel.

A.io: Compare and contrast risk factors, management, and complications of arteriosclerosis and atherosclerosis.
A.q: A 66-year-old man with a prior heart attack and symptomatic peripheral arterial disease takes a maximal statin, and his low-density lipoprotein is 82 mg/dL. Which change is inappropriate at this point?
opts: Rechecking lipids after the change
Lipids are repeated 4 to 12 weeks after any adjustment to judge percentage response, which is appropriate.
Adding evolocumab before ezetimibe
Correct. If the injectable class is considered, ezetimibe is added to the maximal statin before it; skipping that step is out of sequence and less cost-effective.
Continuing the maximal statin
The maximal statin stays in place; nonstatin drugs are added on top of it rather than substituted for it.
Adding ezetimibe to the statin
Adding ezetimibe is the reasonable next step when low-density lipoprotein stays 70 or more on a maximal statin.

A.q: A 48-year-old Black man develops lip and tongue swelling three months after starting an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor. What should be known about this?
opts: An angiotensin receptor blocker carries no risk whatsoever
Angioedema with an angiotensin receptor blocker remains possible, although substitution is usually appropriate.
A beta blocker is the appropriate substitution
The usual substitution is an angiotensin receptor blocker, and beta blockers are not first-line for uncomplicated hypertension.
It is a dose-related effect that resolves on dose reduction
It is a class effect rather than a dose phenomenon, and the agent is stopped rather than reduced.
It is two to four times more common in this group

Correct. It is a bradykinin-mediated class effect of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibition. Angiotensin receptor blockers can usually be used instead, though angioedema with them remains possible. An angiotensin receptor blocker is usually substituted.

A.io: Aortic regurgitation
A.q: A 58-year-old man with a known aortic dissection develops sudden aortic regurgitation with cardiogenic shock and pulmonary edema. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Emergency valve replacement or repair

Correct. Acute severe aortic regurgitation is treated with emergency aortic valve replacement or repair, ideally within 24 hours. Acute causes include myocardial infarction, endocarditis, aortic dissection and trauma.
Percutaneous balloon valve dilation
Balloon procedures open stenotic valves; they do not stop a valve from leaking. Acute severe aortic regurgitation is treated with emergency valve replacement or repair.
Outpatient afterload reduction therapy
Afterload reduction is medical management for chronic aortic regurgitation with preserved ejection fraction or no symptoms. Acute severe regurgitation in shock needs emergency surgery.
Repeat echocardiogram in six months
Surveillance suits mild chronic disease, not a patient in cardiogenic shock. Acute severe aortic regurgitation needs emergency valve replacement or repair.

A.io: Pulmonic stenosis
A.q: A 33-year-old man with severe pulmonic stenosis awaiting valvuloplasty has ankle swelling and an enlarged liver from right heart failure. Which medication relieves these symptoms?
opts: Nitroprusside
Nitroprusside is intravenous stabilization for acute severe aortic regurgitation in intensive care. His right heart failure is treated with a diuretic.
Warfarin
Warfarin is lifelong anticoagulation for a mechanical valve and does nothing for edema. Right heart failure symptoms are relieved with a diuretic.
A nitrate
Nitrates are named in this topic only as a drug to avoid in aortic stenosis. Right heart failure symptoms in pulmonic stenosis are relieved with a diuretic.
A diuretic
Correct. In severe symptomatic pulmonic stenosis, diuretics give symptomatic relief of right heart failure, alongside pulmonic balloon valvuloplasty for the valve itself.

A.io: Acute coronary syndrome
A.q: A 34-year-old man has chest tightness the morning after a long-distance run that left his leg muscles sore. The team wants a blood marker specific to heart muscle. Which marker should be measured?
opts: Smooth-muscle troponin
Smooth muscle cells contain no troponin at all; troponins belong to cardiac and skeletal muscle. The heart-specific marker is troponin I.
Troponin C
Troponin C is one of the three troponin types but is not the heart-specific one. Troponin I is specific to the heart, which matters after skeletal muscle strain.
Any troponin type
Troponins occur in both cardiac and skeletal muscle, so the type matters after a long run. Troponin I is the heart-specific troponin.
Troponin I

Correct. Troponins are proteins of cardiac and skeletal muscle, and there are three types (I, T and C), but troponin I is the one specific to the heart, so skeletal muscle injury from his run does not confound it.

A.q: A 45-year-old woman has recurrent faints with a prodrome, but after a careful history the source is still uncertain. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Begin midodrine empirically
Midodrine is best with neurogenic syncope; starting it without a diagnosis treats a guess rather than the cause.
Refer to the right specialty
Correct. History is the most important portion of diagnosing reflex syncope, or of referring to the right specialty for confirmation when it stays uncertain.
Tell her the faints are harmless
An uncertain source needs confirmation rather than reassurance, because treatment targets the real diagnosis.
Start a vasopressor at home
Vasopressors are reserved for the emergency department and intensive care and would not clarify the source.

A.topic: ST-elevation infarction and right ventricular infarct
A.io: ST segment elevation
A.q: Which drug is avoided in a right ventricular infarct?
opts: Clopidogrel
Clopidogrel is a P2Y12 antagonist given once catheterization is confirmed. The drug to avoid in a right ventricular infarct is nitroglycerin.
Aspirin
Chewable aspirin is given in every ST-elevation infarction, right ventricular or not. The drug to avoid in a right ventricular infarct is nitroglycerin.
Nitroglycerin

Correct. In a right ventricular infarct nitroglycerin is not given: lowering preload removes the Frank-Starling support the failing right ventricle depends on, dropping output and precipitating shock.
Heparin
A heparin drip is given once catheterization is confirmed, whatever the territory. The drug to avoid in a right ventricular infarct is nitroglycerin.

A.q: A 66-year-old woman with long-standing diabetes fainted after walking to the bathroom. Supine she is 146/84 with a heart rate of 70; after 3 minutes standing she is 118/70 with a heart rate of 72. What does her heart rate response indicate?
opts: An arrhythmia is present
An arrhythmia is suggested by abrupt collapse with palpitations and is shown on an electrocardiogram, not by a flat heart rate response.
The autonomic response has failed
Correct. A pressure fall with only a minimal heart rate rise means the sympathetic reflex is not compensating, which favors neurogenic orthostatic hypotension.
Volume depletion is the cause
Volume depletion is usually accompanied by a significant compensatory heart rate rise, which she does not show.
The autonomic response is intact
An intact response produces a significant heart rate rise as pressure falls, as seen with volume loss; hers rose by only 2 beats.

A.q: A 63-year-old woman has right-sided heart failure confirmed by echocardiogram. Her team now wants to know how hemodynamically severe it is. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Troponin trend over a day
Troponin addresses infarction or ischemic cardiomyopathy. Severity is measured by right heart catheterization.
Chest radiograph series
A radiograph shows effusions and heart size but not hemodynamics. Severity is measured by right heart catheterization.
Repeat echocardiogram
The echocardiogram made the diagnosis by ejection fraction. Hemodynamic severity is measured by right heart catheterization.
Right heart catheterization
Correct. Once right-sided failure is established, right heart catheterization measures its hemodynamic severity. The echocardiogram has already made the diagnosis.

A.q: A 68-year-old man hospitalized with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction asks why a defibrillator is being discussed. Which cause accounts for about half of cardiac arrests in hospitalized patients like him?
opts: Ventricular arrhythmias

Correct. About 52% of cardiac arrests in hospitalized patients with reduced ejection fraction are due to ventricular arrhythmias, which is the reason for defibrillator protection in those who meet the criteria.
Complete heart block
Complete heart block is not the leading cause of these arrests. About half of these cardiac arrests are due to ventricular arrhythmias.
Low potassium alone
Electrolytes matter on diuretics, but about half of these cardiac arrests are due to ventricular arrhythmias.
Acute pulmonary embolism
Pulmonary embolism is not the leading cause of these arrests. About half of these cardiac arrests are due to ventricular arrhythmias.

A.io: Identify medical care strategies for coronary artery disease in the lecture topic list for the following populations.
A.q: A 46-year-old woman with microvascular angina asks which factor tends to go along with her episodes. Her coronary arteries were normal on angiography. What should she be told?
opts: Cocaine or amphetamine use
Cocaine and amphetamine are drugs that precipitate vasospastic angina, not the association described for microvascular angina, which is stress or anxiety.
The hours after midnight
Episodes between midnight and early morning describe vasospastic angina. Microvascular angina is often associated with stress or anxiety and is more frequent in women.
Stress or anxiety

Correct. Microvascular angina is more frequent in women and is often associated with stress or anxiety. Proposed mechanisms include endothelial dysfunction, insulin resistance and estrogen deficiency.
Triptan migraine therapy
Triptans can precipitate vasospastic angina and are avoided in it. The factor described for microvascular angina is stress or anxiety.

A.io: Aortic stenosis
A.q: A 74-year-old man with untreated severe aortic stenosis now has breathlessness on exertion, orthopnea (breathlessness lying flat) and ankle swelling. Without valve replacement, which average survival is expected from this symptom?
opts: About 2 years
Correct. Of the cardinal symptoms, heart failure or exertional dyspnea is the most common and carries the worst prognosis, about 2 years. Angina carries about 5 years and syncope about 3 years.
About 10 years
A decade is far too long; once aortic stenosis becomes symptomatic, prognosis is severely worsened. With heart failure symptoms the average survival is about 2 years.
About 5 years
About 5 years is the average survival once angina appears. Heart failure symptoms such as exertional dyspnea and orthopnea carry the worst prognosis, about 2 years.
About 3 years
About 3 years belongs to exertional syncope. Heart failure or exertional dyspnea is the most common cardinal symptom and has the shortest survival, about 2 years.

A.io: Angina pectoris
A.q: A 60-year-old woman has episodes of jaw and tooth pain when she walks uphill that ease when she rests. Her dentist found no dental cause. Which is the most likely cause of her pain?
opts: Pancreatitis
Pancreatic pain goes straight through to the back and is not exertional. Jaw and tooth pain with exertion that eases with rest is referred cardiac pain.
Aortic dissection
Aortic dissection refers pain to the left or interscapular region and is not a recurrent exertional pattern. Referral to the jaw and teeth fits ischemia.
Gallbladder disease
Gallbladder pain refers to the right scapular region and is not brought on by walking uphill. Exertional jaw and tooth pain is referred ischemic pain.
Myocardial ischemia
Correct. Exertional pain relieved by rest is ischemic, and acute coronary syndrome refers pain most commonly to the jaw, tooth or arm. Toothache is even listed among the descriptors of angina.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atherosclerosis and lipid disorders: 1. Hypertriglyceridemia 2. Hypercholesterolemia 3. HDL cholesterol 4. LDL and VLDL cholesterol
A.q: A 42-year-old woman has low-density lipoprotein of 290 mg/dL with a normal triglyceride. She has firm nodules along both Achilles tendons (tendon xanthomas), and her father had a heart attack at 48. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Severe hypertriglyceridemia
Severe hypertriglyceridemia means triglyceride above 500 mg/dL, usually without raised low-density lipoprotein, the reverse of her panel.
Mixed dyslipidemia
Mixed dyslipidemia raises triglyceride above 150 as well as low-density lipoprotein; her triglyceride is normal.
Heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia

Correct. Low-density lipoprotein of 200 to 400 mg/dL, normal triglyceride, Achilles tendon xanthomas (present in about 75%) and premature coronary disease in a first-degree relative fit one mutant allele.
Homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia
The homozygous form presents in childhood with total cholesterol of about 400 to above 1000 mg/dL and atherosclerosis before puberty.

A.q: A 61-year-old with abrupt severe interscapular pain has symmetric, normal-volume pulses in all four limbs. What follows?
opts: Dissection is excluded and another cause should be sought
Symmetric pulses do not exclude it; the clinical suspicion still drives imaging.
An aortic regurgitation murmur would be required to proceed
A murmur is one supporting finding among several, not a prerequisite for imaging.
Normal pulses do not exclude dissection
Correct. Absent pulse findings specifically do not exclude the diagnosis, which is why a normal pulse examination must not close the question. Imaging is still driven by the clinical suspicion.
A normal chest radiograph would then exclude it
A normal chest radiograph does not exclude dissection either, so neither finding can close the question.

A.q: A 70-year-old man with chronic left-sided heart failure develops right-sided failure. He asks what this means for his outlook. Which reply is accurate?
opts: His prognosis is now much worse
Correct. Right-sided failure carries a much worse prognosis than left-sided failure, and in him it marks progression of chronic left-sided disease.
It improves once edema clears
Clearing edema relieves symptoms but does not change the outlook: right-sided failure carries a much worse prognosis.
His prognosis is now better
The comparison runs the other way. Right-sided failure carries a much worse prognosis than left-sided failure.
His prognosis is unchanged
The outlook does change: right-sided failure carries a much worse prognosis than left-sided failure.

A.io: Mitral regurgitation
A.q: A 64-year-old man, three days after an acute myocardial infarction, has sudden breathlessness, crackles in both lungs and a new holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla. Which is the most likely cause?
opts: Tricuspid annular dilation
Tricuspid annular dilation causes tricuspid regurgitation in pulmonary hypertension, heard at the lower sternal border. An apical murmur after infarction is papillary muscle rupture.
Papillary muscle rupture

Correct. An acute myocardial infarction with papillary muscle rupture is an acute cause of mitral regurgitation, and acute mitral regurgitation presents with left-sided heart failure symptoms such as dyspnea and rales.
Myxomatous degeneration
Myxomatous degeneration causes mitral valve prolapse, a chronic cause of mitral regurgitation. The sudden murmur three days after an infarction points to papillary muscle rupture.
Rheumatic heart disease
Rheumatic heart disease is a cause of mitral regurgitation, but it does not arrive suddenly three days after an infarction. Papillary muscle rupture does.

A.topic: Post-infarction care and sudden cardiac death
A.io: Acute myocardial infraction
A.q: A 59-year-old man is ready for discharge after an ST-elevation myocardial infarction. His echocardiogram shows an ejection fraction of 35%, and his heart rate is 78/min with no bradycardia. Which drug class improves his survival?
opts: Glycoprotein 2b/3a inhibitor
Glycoprotein 2b/3a inhibitors have fallen out of favor and are not a survival therapy after discharge. With a reduced ejection fraction, the class that improves survival is the beta blocker.
Beta blocker

Correct. After an infarction that leaves the ejection fraction reduced, a beta blocker improves survival, so it belongs in his discharge regimen unless bradycardia or another contraindication is present. With preserved function that benefit is not established.
Calcium channel blocker

Calcium channel blockers, diltiazem and verapamil included, do not improve survival after infarction; they relieve angina when a beta blocker cannot be used. Beta blockers improve survival when the ejection fraction is reduced.
Sublingual nitroglycerin
Sublingual nitroglycerin relieves anginal pain as needed but carries no survival claim. With a reduced ejection fraction, the post-infarction class that improves survival is the beta blocker.

A.q: A 70-year-old man with orthostatic hypotension keeps standing up quickly despite being told not to, because he does not see why it matters. Which approach most improves his adherence?
opts: Explain why the pressure falls
Correct. Understanding is the key to compliance: once a patient knows why the pressure falls on standing, slow position changes make sense and are followed.
Add a vasopressor at home
Vasopressors are for the emergency department and intensive care only and do not address adherence.
Repeat the same instruction
Repeating an instruction without the reason rarely changes behavior; understanding is what drives compliance.
Stop discussing it with him
Dropping education abandons the most important tool; patient education is central to managing hypotension.

A.io: Differentiate between systolic dysfunction and diastolic dysfunction..
A.q: Which heart sound belongs to diastolic heart failure?
opts: An opening snap
An opening snap belongs to mitral stenosis, a cause of right-sided failure. Diastolic failure gives a fourth heart sound.
A pericardial rub
A rub is not part of the heart failure chain. Diastolic failure gives a fourth heart sound from atrial contraction against a stiff ventricle.
Third heart sound
A third heart sound is rapid filling of a dilated left ventricle, which belongs to the systolic chain. Diastolic failure gives a fourth heart sound.
Fourth heart sound
Correct. A fourth heart sound is strong left atrial contraction against a stiff, hypertrophied left ventricle, and it sits in the diastolic chain with hypertension and edema that starts peripherally.

A.io: Compare and contrast precipitating factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis (including role of B-type natriuretic peptide, BNP), and treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
A.q: A 67-year-old woman with heart failure has cool, clammy extremities, a narrow pulse pressure and sleepiness, along with orthopnea (breathlessness lying flat) and leg edema. Which bedside hemodynamic profile fits?
opts: Cold and wet
Correct. Low-perfusion signs (cool extremities, narrow pulse pressure, obtundation) plus congestion signs (orthopnea, edema) place her in the cold and wet profile, hypoperfusion with congestion.
Warm and wet
Warm and wet is congestion with adequate perfusion. Her cool extremities, narrow pulse pressure and sleepiness mean perfusion is low, so she is cold and wet.
Cold and dry
Cold and dry is low perfusion without congestion. Her orthopnea and edema mean she is congested, so she is cold and wet.
Warm and dry
Warm and dry is the normal profile. She has both low perfusion and congestion, so she is cold and wet.

A.io: Acute myocardial infraction
A.q: Which test shows a regional wall motion abnormality?
opts: Chest radiograph
A chest radiograph is part of every chest pain workup, but it shows the lungs and silhouette, not wall movement. Wall motion is seen on an echocardiogram.
Calcium score
A computed tomography calcium score stratifies long-term risk and does not show movement. Regional wall motion is assessed on an echocardiogram.
Echocardiogram
Correct. Regional wall motion abnormalities (hypokinesia, akinesia, dyskinesia) are seen on an echocardiogram, which images the moving walls of the ventricle segment by segment.
Troponin I level
Troponin I shows myocardial injury in the blood, not how a wall moves. Hypokinesia, akinesia and dyskinesia are seen on an echocardiogram.

A.q: A 14-year-old girl with homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia remains severely elevated despite a high-intensity statin, ezetimibe and regular apheresis. Which adjunct is approved at her age?
opts: Evinacumab
Correct. Evinacumab, an intravenous monoclonal antibody that lowers low-density lipoprotein and triglyceride, is adjunct therapy for patients 12 years and older with the homozygous disorder.
Colesevelam
Colesevelam is a bile acid sequestrant for extra low-density lowering, not the adjunct approved for homozygous disease from age 12.
Gemfibrozil
Gemfibrozil is a fibrate for triglyceride, which is normal in familial hypercholesterolemia.
Fish oil
Fish oil is associated with lower coronary death in general, but it is not an adjunct for the homozygous disorder.

A.io: Compare and contrast anticoagulation therapy for prosthetic heart valves.
A.q: Which drug is the most commonly used vitamin K antagonist for a mechanical valve?
opts: Heparin
Heparin is not a vitamin K antagonist; it is the bridging agent used around surgery. The most common vitamin K antagonist is warfarin.
Warfarin

Correct. Warfarin is the most commonly used vitamin K antagonist, the long-term anticoagulant for mechanical heart valves; if surgery requires heparin instead, warfarin is bridged until the ratio is therapeutic.
Aspirin
Aspirin is an antiplatelet agent, and antiplatelets are ranked below vitamin K antagonists for mechanical valves. The vitamin K antagonist is warfarin.
Clopidogrel
Clopidogrel is an antiplatelet agent, not a vitamin K antagonist. The most commonly used vitamin K antagonist is warfarin.

A.q: Which drug combinations are preferred as initial therapy?
opts: A beta blocker with a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker
This pairing risks severe bradycardia and heart block because both slow nodal conduction.
An angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor with an angiotensin receptor blocker
This combination is specifically prohibited: dual renin-angiotensin blockade raises hyperkalemia and kidney injury risk without additional benefit.
Two thiazide-type diuretics together
Combining agents of the same class adds adverse effects without the complementary mechanism that the preferred pairings provide.
A renin-angiotensin blocker with a calcium blocker or diuretic

Correct, because the classes act by complementary mechanisms. A single-pill combination is preferred where two agents are started, since it improves adherence. That means an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker paired with a dihydropyridine or a thiazide-type diuretic.

A.io: Distinguish between acute and chronic hypotension
A.q: A 34-year-old man is brought in after taking a large quantity of a relative's blood pressure pills. His pressure dropped suddenly over the past hour and he is dizzy. How is his hypotension best classified?
opts: Long-lasting acute infectious hypotension
Infection causes long-lasting acute hypotension, and nothing here suggests bacteremia or sepsis.
Chronic hypotension from a cardiac cause
Chronic hypotension comes from cardiogenic causes such as cardiomyopathy and waxes and wanes over time.
Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension is a postural fall from autonomic failure, not a sudden drop after an overdose.
Acute hypotension from a toxic cause
Correct. Medication-mediated overdose is a toxic cause of acute hypotension, which is of sudden onset, usually symptomatic and tied to a specific trigger.

A.q: A 69-year-old woman with reduced ejection fraction (fraction 27%) has blood pressure above goal on her heart failure regimen. Verapamil is proposed. What is the most appropriate response?
opts: Avoid it and use recommended classes
Correct. Verapamil is a calcium channel blocker, and calcium channel blockers are avoided in heart failure. Pressure control comes from optimizing the recommended classes as tolerated.
Use it in place of her beta blocker
Replacing a core beta blocker with a calcium channel blocker is backwards; the calcium channel blocker is avoided in heart failure.
Start it as first-line pressure control
Calcium channel blockers are not first-line in heart failure; they are avoided. The recommended classes are optimized instead.
Add it once she reaches class IV
Advancing class does not make calcium channel blockers appropriate. They are avoided in heart failure at every class.

A.q: A 22-year-old man is found to have a blood pressure of 158/92 in both arms. His femoral pulses are weak and delayed relative to the radial pulses, and his leg systolic pressure is lower than his arm pressure. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Primary hypertension
Onset this early, with an abnormal pulse examination, points away from primary hypertension and toward a structural cause.
Coarctation of the aorta

Correct. Leg systolic normally EXCEEDS arm systolic, so a reversal is the abnormal finding, and radial-femoral delay places a structural obstruction between the two territories. Early onset hypertension is itself a clue to a secondary cause.
Primary aldosteronism
Aldosteronism is screened for in early or resistant hypertension, but it does not alter the femoral pulses or the arm-to-leg pressure relationship.
Renovascular disease from fibromuscular dysplasia
Fibromuscular dysplasia causes early-onset hypertension in young patients, but through renal artery narrowing, which produces an abdominal bruit rather than radial-femoral delay.

A.q: What is the treatment of choice in homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia?
opts: Low-density lipoprotein apheresis
Correct. Apheresis, like dialysis, is the elective removal of low-density particles from the circulation; most patients also need more than one drug, starting with high-intensity statins.
Lifestyle and dietary change alone
Lifestyle cannot correct a receptor defect with total cholesterol of about 400 to above 1000 mg/dL.
Fibrate monotherapy with diet
Triglyceride is normal in familial hypercholesterolemia, so a fibrate targets the wrong lipid.
Moderate-intensity statin alone
Moderate intensity is far too weak; high-intensity statins are the usual drug regimen alongside apheresis.

A.io: Mitral stenosis
A.q: A 45-year-old woman with rheumatic mitral stenosis is in sinus rhythm. Which electrocardiogram finding is most expected?
opts: Right axis deviation alone
Right axis deviation with right ventricular hypertrophy is the electrocardiogram of pulmonic stenosis. Mitral stenosis shows left atrial abnormality first.
Left atrial abnormality

Correct. Mitral stenosis raises left atrial size and pressure, so the electrocardiogram shows left atrial abnormality. Atrial fibrillation is common in severe disease, and right ventricular hypertrophy appears with pulmonary hypertension.
Right atrial enlargement only
Right atrial enlargement out of proportion to right ventricular hypertrophy is the tricuspid stenosis pattern. Mitral stenosis shows left atrial abnormality.
An expected normal tracing
Mitral stenosis enlarges the left atrium, and the electrocardiogram reflects that as left atrial abnormality. A normal tracing is not what is expected.

A.q: A 54-year-old woman with dyslipidemia weighs 200 pounds and asks how much weight she should aim to lose. Which goal is most appropriate?
opts: About 60 to 80 pounds
That is 30% to 40% of her weight, far beyond the 5% to 10% reduction set by the lifestyle plan.
No weight loss is needed
Obesity raises hepatic very-low-density production, and a 5% to 10% loss is part of treatment.
About 10 to 20 pounds
Correct. Therapeutic lifestyle changes aim for a 5% to 10% reduction of initial weight; for 200 pounds that is 10 to 20 pounds.
About 1 to 2 pounds
One to two pounds is only 0.5% to 1% of her weight, well short of the 5% to 10% goal.

A.q: A 60-year-old woman without diabetes has a 10-year atherosclerotic risk of 11% and an uncertain statin decision. She has never smoked and has no family history of premature disease. Her coronary artery calcium score is zero. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Withhold or delay the statin
Correct. A calcium score of zero lowers risk, so statin therapy may be withheld or delayed, except in cigarette smokers, diabetes or a strong family history of premature disease.
Add ezetimibe now
Ezetimibe is an add-on to a maximal statin in very high-risk disease, not a primary-prevention starter.
Start a high-intensity statin
High intensity is for clinical disease, very high low-density lipoprotein or high 10-year risk, not a zero calcium score.
Order a skin biopsy
Skin biopsy confirms homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia and plays no part in this decision.

A.q: A 50-year-old man has low-density lipoprotein of 178 mg/dL. He reports fatigue, weight gain and cold intolerance over the past year. Before a statin is started, which test should be ordered?
opts: Fasting triglyceride only
Triglyceride is part of his profile, but his symptoms point to hypothyroidism, which raises low-density lipoprotein.
Thyroid function tests
Correct. Decreased thyroid hormone down-regulates hepatic low-density lipoprotein receptors and raises low-density lipoprotein, so elevated levels call for screening for low thyroid before a statin.
Coronary artery calcium score
Calcium scoring helps an uncertain intermediate-risk statin decision; a treatable secondary cause must be excluded first.
Skin biopsy for receptor activity
Skin biopsy confirms homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia in childhood; his picture suggests a secondary cause.

A.q: A 72-year-old man has diabetic autonomic neuropathy and also congestive heart failure. He faints on standing. Which of the following should be avoided?
opts: Treating the underlying cause
Treating the underlying condition is the central principle for orthostasis and is never avoided.
Slow position changes
Slow positional changes are first-line for orthostatic syncope and are safe alongside heart failure.
Fludrocortisone
Correct. Fludrocortisone causes salt and water retention and is avoided in congestive heart failure, even though it is best with the tachycardia syndrome.
A careful history
History is the most important part of diagnosing the source of orthostatic syncope and is always appropriate.

A.io: Pulmonic regurgitation
A.q: What is the Graham Steell murmur?
opts: Tricuspid regurgitation's inspiratory murmur
The inspiratory increase of the holosystolic tricuspid regurgitation murmur is the Carvallo sign, not the Graham Steell murmur.
Pulmonic regurgitation's early diastolic murmur

Correct. The Graham Steell murmur is the brief, high-pitched, early diastolic decrescendo murmur of pulmonic regurgitation at the left second intercostal space, radiating to the mid-right sternal border with full inspiration.
Aortic stenosis's harsh systolic murmur
The harsh systolic ejection murmur radiating to the carotids is aortic stenosis. The Graham Steell murmur is pulmonic regurgitation, early in diastole.
Tricuspid stenosis's mid-diastolic rumble
The mid-diastolic rumble near the xiphoid is tricuspid stenosis. The Graham Steell murmur is the early diastolic pulmonic regurgitation murmur.

A.io: Differentiate each stage of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA), natural history classification of heart failure, and associated treatment recommendations of each stage.
A.q: A 57-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes has asymptomatic left ventricular hypertrophy on echocardiogram. She already takes an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor. Which drug class should be added for her diabetes-related risk?
opts: Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor
Correct. She is stage B, and stage B carries a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor for patients with diabetes as well as the converting enzyme inhibitor and a beta blocker.
Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist
The antagonist belongs to symptomatic heart failure. In stage B with diabetes the added class is the sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
Calcium channel blocker such as amlodipine
Calcium channel blockers are avoided in heart failure. In stage B with diabetes the added class is the sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
Angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor
The neprilysin combination belongs to symptomatic reduced ejection fraction in functional class II or III. Stage B with diabetes adds a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.

A.q: Which family history counts as premature coronary heart disease?
opts: A male first-degree relative before 65
65 is the cutoff for a female first-degree relative; for a male relative the threshold is before 55 years old.
Any second-degree relative before 70
Only first-degree relatives count, with coronary disease before 55 in a male and before 65 in a female.
A female first-degree relative before 55
55 is the male cutoff; a female first-degree relative counts if her coronary disease began before 65.
A male first-degree relative before 55
Correct. Premature coronary heart disease means disease in a male first-degree relative before 55 or a female first-degree relative before 65.

A.q: A 67-year-old woman presents with fatigue, breathlessness with exertion and new ankle edema. Which blood test best supports a clinical diagnosis of heart failure?
opts: Complete blood count
The blood count helps with the differential, for example anemia, but does not support the diagnosis itself. The natriuretic peptide does.
B-type natriuretic peptide
Correct. Heart failure is a clinical diagnosis: signs and symptoms plus an elevated natriuretic peptide or objective congestion. The peptide is the laboratory test that carries that weight.
Serum potassium
Potassium is followed for therapy safety. The natriuretic peptide supports the diagnosis of heart failure.
Cardiac troponin
Troponin is ordered when infarction or ischemic cardiomyopathy is a concern. The natriuretic peptide supports the diagnosis of heart failure.

A.q: A 71-year-old man had his diuretic dose increased 10 days ago. He now has lightheadedness on standing, a 28 mmHg systolic fall and a heart rate rise from 70 to 94. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Reduce the recently increased diuretic
Correct. The offending agent is removed first: iatrogenic hypotension is treated by reducing or removing the medication, with slow position changes meanwhile.
Start fludrocortisone
Fludrocortisone is best with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome and retains salt and water; it does not address the diuretic.
Start midodrine for the pressure
Midodrine is best with neurogenic syncope. Here the cause is a medication, which is reduced rather than counteracted with another drug.
Add droxidopa as an adjunct
Droxidopa has mild efficacy and is used as an adjunct to midodrine or fludrocortisone, not to offset a diuretic side effect.

A.io: Unstable
A.q: A 63-year-old man has had chest pressure at rest for two days. His electrocardiogram shows inverted T waves, and two standard troponin I levels are 0.01 ng/mL. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: ST-elevation infarction
An ST-elevation myocardial infarction shows ST elevation above 1 mm in two or more leads with elevated troponin I. His tracing shows only inverted T waves and his troponin I is not abnormal.
Infarction without ST elevation
A non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction needs an elevated troponin I, meaning standard troponin I above 0.04 ng/mL. His two values of 0.01 ng/mL are not abnormal, so this is unstable angina.
Unstable angina
Correct. Pain at rest with nonspecific electrocardiogram changes, usually inverted T waves, and a normal troponin I is unstable angina. A standard troponin I at or below 0.04 ng/mL is not abnormal.
Stable angina
Stable angina is brought on by exertion and relieved by rest and nitroglycerin. Pain that now occurs at rest has become unstable angina, an acute coronary syndrome.

A.q: A 63-year-old man with exertional chest pressure has a nuclear stress test that is abnormal. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Repeat the stress test
Repeating an abnormal nuclear study only delays the answer. An abnormal nuclear stress test goes on to cardiac catheterization.
Cardiac catheterization
Correct. An abnormal nuclear stress test leads to cardiac catheterization, where coronary angiography, the gold standard for diagnosing coronary artery disease, defines the lesions.
Discharge with no follow-up
An abnormal nuclear stress test is not a result to walk away from. It is followed by cardiac catheterization to look at the coronary arteries.
Coronary calcium score
A calcium score adds risk stratification, not anatomy, and does not follow an abnormal stress test. The next step is cardiac catheterization.

A.q: A 59-year-old man remains at 158/96 on three agents at maximally tolerated doses. What is the commonest explanation to exclude first?
opts: Undiagnosed primary aldosteronism
Secondary hypertension is on the list to rule out, but nonadherence is the commonest single explanation for apparent resistance.
Medication nonadherence
Correct, and it heads a list that also includes measurement error, white coat effect, high sodium or alcohol intake, interfering drugs, and undiagnosed sleep apnea or secondary hypertension.
An incorrectly sized cuff
Measurement error belongs on the list, but nonadherence is specifically named as commonest.
Progressive renal artery stenosis
Renovascular disease is one secondary cause to consider, but it is not the commonest reason control appears resistant.

B.q: A 38-year-old man has low-density lipoprotein of 260 mg/dL, normal triglyceride and firm nodules over the extensor tendons of his hands (tendon xanthomas). His brother had a heart attack at 44. Which drug regimen is started first?
opts: High-intensity statin

Correct. The common regimen in heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia is a high-intensity statin, with ezetimibe and nicotinic acid added if needed and aggressive reduction of other vascular risk factors.
Low-intensity statin
Low intensity lowers low-density lipoprotein under 30%, far too little for a receptor defect with levels of 200 to 400.
Evolocumab alone
Evolocumab is reserved for patients refractory to drug therapy, after high-intensity statins, not as the opening regimen.
Fibrate therapy
Fibrates are the most effective triglyceride-lowering drugs; his triglyceride is normal and the problem is low-density lipoprotein.

B.q: A 66-year-old African American man with reduced ejection fraction (fraction 25%) remains short of breath with slight exertion despite optimized sacubitril-valsartan, a beta blocker, spironolactone and dapagliflozin. Which addition is recommended?
opts: Dobutamine continued at home
Dobutamine is an inotrope for intensive care use only. The recommended outpatient addition is hydralazine with isosorbide dinitrate.
Isosorbide mononitrate on its own
The recommendation pairs hydralazine with isosorbide dinitrate. A nitrate alone is not the recommended addition for class III or IV.
Hydralazine with isosorbide dinitrate

Correct. For African American patients with reduced ejection fraction in functional class III or IV, hydralazine with nitrates carries a strong recommendation on top of the core classes. Slight-exertion symptoms put him in functional class III.
Verapamil for additional rate control
Verapamil is a calcium channel blocker, which is avoided in heart failure. His class III disease qualifies for hydralazine with isosorbide dinitrate.

B.q: How does aortic dissection classically present?
opts: Episodic headache with sweating and palpitations
That pattern of episodic headache, sweating and palpitations suggests pheochromocytoma among the secondary causes rather than an acute aortic event.
Abrupt severe chest or back pain, maximal at onset
Correct, and maximal at onset is the discriminating feature: pain that builds is less characteristic than pain that arrives at full intensity immediately. Patients often describe it as tearing.
Painless progressive dyspnea
Dissection is characteristically painful, with pain that is abrupt, severe and maximal at onset.
Gradually worsening chest pain over several days
The pain is abrupt and maximal at onset rather than building gradually, which is one of the features that distinguishes it.

B.q: A 55-year-old man with hypertensive retinopathy achieves good blood pressure control. What can be expected of his retinal findings?
opts: The changes will progress regardless of control
Progression is not inevitable, and regression of the retinopathy with good control is described.
The changes are permanent once established
Control of hypertension can produce regression of retinopathy, so the finding is not a fixed one.
Control can lead to regression of the retinopathy
Correct, so the finding is both a prognostic marker and something that can improve with treatment. Retinopathy predicts long-term stroke risk independently of the pressure level.
The changes have no relationship to blood pressure
Retinal changes are a direct consequence of the pressure, and they predict long-term stroke risk.

B.io: ST segment elevation
B.q: A 57-year-old woman has chest pain with ST elevation in leads I, aVL, V5 and V6. Which artery is the most likely culprit?
opts: Posterior interventricular
The posterior interventricular branch supplies the posteromedial papillary muscle and the inferior wall. Lateral leads point to the left circumflex artery.
Right coronary artery
The right coronary artery is the culprit for the inferior leads II, III and aVF. Leads I, aVL, V5 and V6 are lateral, pointing to the circumflex.
Left circumflex artery
Correct. Leads I, aVL, V5 and V6 are the lateral leads, and lateral ST elevation points to the left circumflex artery (or a diagonal branch of the left anterior descending artery).
Right marginal branch
The right marginal branch arises from the right coronary artery along the right ventricle. Lateral ST elevation in I, aVL, V5 and V6 points to the circumflex.

B.q: A 71-year-old woman with resistant hypertension is started on lisinopril. Her creatinine rises markedly within a week. What does this suggest?
opts: Bilateral renal artery stenosis

Correct. Where perfusion depends on angiotensin-mediated efferent arteriolar tone, blocking it drops the filtration pressure sharply. This is one of the recognized clues to renovascular disease, and it is why the agent is contraindicated in bilateral stenosis. A hemodynamically significant unilateral stenosis does the same.
Expected drug effect requiring no change in approach
A small early creatinine rise can be acceptable, but a MARKED rise specifically points toward renovascular disease rather than being dismissed.
Progression of underlying diabetic nephropathy
Diabetic nephropathy declines over months to years rather than jumping within a week of starting a renin-angiotensin blocker.
Acute interstitial nephritis from the medication
Interstitial nephritis is not the mechanism described for this pattern; the abrupt rise on renin-angiotensin blockade points to renal artery stenosis.

B.io: Compare and contrast precipitating factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis (including role of B-type natriuretic peptide, BNP), and treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
B.q: A 75-year-old man with heart failure diagnosed three years ago has had four days of worsening orthopnea (breathlessness lying flat) and leg swelling. How is this episode classified?
opts: Acute new-onset heart failure
New-onset failure is a first symptomatic episode. He has had heart failure for three years, so this is acute on chronic heart failure.
High-output heart failure
Nothing suggests anemia, hyperthyroidism or a fistula. This is a sudden worsening of chronic disease, acute on chronic heart failure.
Pre-heart failure, stage B
Pre-heart failure is asymptomatic structural disease. He is symptomatic with known chronic disease: acute on chronic heart failure.
Acute on chronic heart failure

Correct. Heart failure present for more than a year is chronic, and a sudden worsening on top of it is acute on chronic heart failure, the last step of the sequence from pre-heart failure through exacerbation.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atherosclerosis and lipid disorders: 1. Hypertriglyceridemia 2. Hypercholesterolemia 3. HDL cholesterol 4. LDL and VLDL cholesterol
B.q: Which dyslipidemia is the most common type seen in clinical practice?
opts: Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia
Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia is described as a rare disorder, caused by an apolipoprotein E mutation.
Mixed dyslipidemia

Correct. Mixed dyslipidemia, elevated triglyceride and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol from genetic predisposition plus medical and environmental factors, is the most common type in clinical practice.
Homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia
The homozygous form occurs in about 1 in 1 million persons worldwide, which makes it rare rather than common.
Familial chylomicronemia syndrome
Familial chylomicronemia syndrome causes severe hypertriglyceridemia with fasting levels usually above 1000 mg/dL; it is a disorder recognized for its danger, not its frequency.

B.io: Acute myocardial infraction
B.q: A 64-year-old man with an inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction suddenly develops complete heart block on the monitor. Which artery is most likely occluded?
opts: Anterior interventricular artery
The anterior interventricular artery (the former left anterior descending) is the most common culprit overall, but it supplies the anterior wall and septum, not the atrioventricular node.
Diagonal artery
The diagonal artery is a lateral branch that helps supply the left ventricle. Complete heart block during an infarct points to the right coronary artery, which supplies the atrioventricular node.
Left circumflex artery

The left circumflex artery can supply the sinoatrial node in a minority of people, but the atrioventricular node is supplied by the right coronary artery, so heart block implicates the right coronary artery.
Right coronary artery

Correct. The right coronary artery supplies the atrioventricular node, so an occlusion that produces complete heart block points to it. That is why right coronary artery infarcts are the ones most likely to cause dysrhythmias.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
B.q: A 21-year-old woman has just been diagnosed with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome after her heart rate rose by 38 within 10 minutes of standing. Which is the most appropriate first treatment?
opts: Restrict salt and fluid
Restriction runs opposite to the treatment, which increases water and salt intake.
Increase water and salt intake
Correct. Increasing water and salt intake is the first listed treatment, with fludrocortisone as the drug best suited to the syndrome.
Begin vasopressin
Vasopressin is a pressor reserved for the emergency department and intensive care, not an outpatient syndrome.
Start midodrine
Midodrine is best with neurogenic syncope, a postural pressure fall from autonomic failure, not this syndrome.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
B.q: Which drug is best suited to postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome?
opts: Fludrocortisone
Correct. Fludrocortisone is best with the tachycardia syndrome; because it causes salt and water retention it is avoided in heart failure.
Midodrine
Midodrine is best with neurogenic syncope and is avoided with supine hypertension, severe heart disease and chronic kidney disease.
Droxidopa
Droxidopa has mild efficacy, is better with supine hypertension, and is usually an adjunct to midodrine or fludrocortisone.
Phenylephrine
Phenylephrine is among the pressors used only in the emergency department and intensive care, not for an outpatient syndrome.

B.io: Mitral valve prolapse
B.q: A 19-year-old woman is found to have a mid-systolic click at the apex at a sports physical. She feels well. Which is the most appropriate initial test?
opts: Cardiac catheterization
Catheterization is invasive and not how prolapse is diagnosed. An echocardiogram shows the thickened, redundant mitral leaflets.
Echocardiogram
Correct. Mitral valve prolapse is diagnosed by echocardiogram, which shows thickened, redundant mitral leaflets greater than 5 mm bowing into the left atrium during systole.
Chest radiograph
A chest radiograph does not show the leaflets or their motion. A mid-systolic click is investigated with an echocardiogram showing redundant leaflets.
Electrocardiogram
An electrocardiogram does not show valve anatomy. The diagnosis of mitral valve prolapse is made by echocardiogram.

B.io: Compare and contrast precipitating factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis (including role of B-type natriuretic peptide, BNP), and treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
B.q: A 58-year-old woman has a week of fatigue and mild breathlessness. Her B-type natriuretic peptide is 250. How should this result be interpreted?
opts: Acute heart failure is ruled out
Rule-out applies only below 100. At 250 the level sits in the indeterminate range of 100 to 400.
Heart failure is likely
Heart failure becomes likely only above 400. At 250 the result sits in the indeterminate range.
Indeterminate for heart failure
Correct. Between 100 and 400 the peptide has no useful sensitivity or specificity for heart failure, so the clinical picture and imaging have to settle the question.
Acute heart failure is likely
Acute heart failure becomes likely only above 900. At 250 the result sits in the indeterminate range.

B.io: Tricuspid stenosis
B.q: A 50-year-old woman has severe symptomatic tricuspid stenosis with leg swelling and jugular venous distension. Before any procedure, which medical regimen is appropriate?
opts: Afterload reduction with hydralazine
Afterload reduction is medical management for chronic aortic regurgitation. Tricuspid stenosis uses low salt, a diuretic and an aldosterone antagonist.
Low salt, diuretic, aldosterone antagonist
Correct. Severe symptomatic tricuspid stenosis is managed with a low-salt diet, diuretics and an aldosterone antagonist, with bioprosthetic valve replacement preferred when the valve is replaced.
Nitrates, beta blocker, calcium blocker
Nitrates, beta blockers and calcium channel blockers are the avoid list for aortic stenosis. Tricuspid stenosis is managed with salt restriction, diuretics and an aldosterone antagonist.
Warfarin with a heparin bridge
Warfarin with heparin bridging is anticoagulation for mechanical valves. Tricuspid stenosis is managed with low salt, a diuretic and an aldosterone antagonist.

B.io: Differentiate between systolic dysfunction and diastolic dysfunction..
B.q: How does dilated cardiomyopathy differ from hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
opts: Thickened muscle that contracts poorly
Thickened muscle contracts strongly and relaxes poorly. Dilated cardiomyopathy is thin, ballooned muscle with poor contraction.
Normal muscle with leaking valves
Valve disease is a separate cause of heart failure. Dilated cardiomyopathy is thin, ballooned muscle that contracts poorly.
Thin, ballooned muscle that contracts poorly
Correct. Dilated cardiomyopathy is decreased muscle with poor contraction and loss of elasticity. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is increased muscle that contracts strongly but relaxes poorly.
Thickened muscle that relaxes poorly
That describes hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, which leads the diastolic chain. Dilated cardiomyopathy is thin and ballooned and contracts poorly.

B.q: A 63-year-old with long-standing hypertension has an estimated filtration rate that has fallen over eighteen months and a rising urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio. He also has type 2 diabetes. What should be done next?
opts: Attribute it all to diabetes and stop antihypertensives
Hypertension injures renal vessels, glomeruli and interstitium, and withdrawing therapy would accelerate the decline.
Conclude the albuminuria is a laboratory artifact
Rising albuminuria and falling filtration are the earliest measurable markers of renal damage and are tracked as trends rather than dismissed.
Evaluate for alternative renal causes too

Correct. Not all chronic kidney disease in a hypertensive patient is hypertensive, and diabetes must be evaluated. The relationship is bidirectional, so the presence of both does not establish which came first.
Attribute it all to hypertension and intensify control
Control matters, but attributing everything to the pressure risks missing a second treatable disease.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atherosclerosis and lipid disorders: 1. Hypertriglyceridemia 2. Hypercholesterolemia 3. HDL cholesterol 4. LDL and VLDL cholesterol
B.q: A 32-year-old man arrives for his first adult screening visit, having eaten lunch an hour ago. What is the most appropriate lipid testing today?
opts: Nothing until after a 12-hour fast
Sending him away to fast delays screening for no benefit; a non-fasting profile is acceptable unless triglyceride is 400 mg/dL or more.
Total and high-density cholesterol only
Limiting a non-fasting visit to these two is the older rule. The whole profile can be drawn after lunch and used for screening.
Triglyceride and nothing else
Triglyceride alone cannot estimate coronary risk. The full non-fasting profile, with total, high-density and low-density values, is what screening needs.
A full non-fasting lipid profile

Correct. Under the 2018 guideline a non-fasting profile, triglyceride and calculated low-density value included, is acceptable for screening; a fast is needed only if triglyceride turns out to be 400 mg/dL or more.

B.io: Pulmonic stenosis
B.q: How does inspiration change the pulmonic stenosis murmur?
opts: It does not change
Right-sided murmurs respond to respiration. Pulmonic stenosis grows louder on inspiration as right-sided preload rises.
It gets louder
Correct. The pulmonic stenosis murmur increases with inspiration, which raises venous return to the right heart, and it comes with a split second heart sound.
It turns diastolic
Respiration changes loudness, not timing. Pulmonic stenosis stays a mid-systolic ejection murmur and grows louder on inspiration.
It gets softer
Softening on inspiration would fit a left-sided murmur. Pulmonic stenosis is right-sided, so inspiration makes it louder.

B.io: Aortic stenosis
B.q: What is the 3-year mortality of symptomatic aortic stenosis?
opts: 35% is the share of patients older than 70 who have aortic stenosis. The 3-year mortality once symptoms appear is 75%.
25% is the share of patients older than 65 who have aortic stenosis. The 3-year mortality of the symptomatic disease is 75%.
Ten percent is far too low. The disease is insidious until late, and once symptomatic its 3-year mortality is 75%.
Correct. Symptomatic aortic stenosis has a 3-year mortality of 75%. Once symptoms begin, prognosis is severely worsened, which is why symptoms suggestive of the disease prompt an echocardiogram.

B.io: Differentiate each stage of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA), natural history classification of heart failure, and associated treatment recommendations of each stage.
B.q: Why is a beta blocker the wrong first choice for an at-risk patient with diabetes and a normal heart?
opts: The first drug is a sodium-glucose inhibitor
Correct. In stage A the only strongly recommended drug is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor in patients with diabetes. The beta blocker is a stage B therapy once structural disease exists.
Diabetes makes any drug unnecessary
Diabetes is exactly what triggers treatment in stage A: a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
Beta blockers are banned in all heart failure
Beta blockers are core therapy in reduced ejection fraction and a stage B recommendation. They are simply not the first choice in stage A.
A loop diuretic must be started first
A stage A patient has no congestion to treat. The first drug is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.

B.io: Aortic regurgitation
B.q: A 63-year-old woman with acute severe aortic regurgitation from endocarditis is waiting for valve surgery that is delayed by several hours. Which is the most appropriate temporary stabilization in the intensive care unit?
opts: Intravenous diuretics and nitroprusside

Correct. If surgery for acute severe aortic regurgitation is delayed, temporary stabilization may be attempted in the intensive care unit with intravenous diuretics and a vasodilator such as nitroprusside.
A fluid bolus to raise her preload
Adding volume worsens the pulmonary edema of acute regurgitation. Temporary stabilization uses intravenous diuretics and a vasodilator such as nitroprusside.
Percutaneous balloon valvuloplasty
Balloon valvuloplasty relieves stenosis in children and young adults; it does not stabilize a leaking valve. The bridge to surgery is intravenous diuretics and nitroprusside.
Oral hydralazine and discharge home
Oral afterload reduction is chronic outpatient therapy. Acute severe regurgitation awaiting surgery is stabilized in intensive care with intravenous diuretics and nitroprusside.

B.io: ST segment elevation
B.q: A 66-year-old man with severe multivessel coronary disease is scheduled for a coronary artery bypass graft. Which conduit is the first choice to bypass his obstructions?
opts: The superficial femoral vein
The superficial femoral vein is not the bypass conduit. Arteries (the mammary or radial) come first, and when a vein must be used it is the great saphenous vein.
A mammary or radial artery
Correct. Bypass grafting anastomoses one or both of the mammary arteries, or a radial artery, to the coronary artery distal to the obstructive lesion. A vein is used only if an artery cannot be used.
The popliteal vein
The popliteal vein is not harvested for bypass. First choice is a mammary or radial artery; the great saphenous vein is the fallback when an artery cannot be used.
The great saphenous vein
The great saphenous vein is the vein used when an artery cannot be, connecting the aorta to the coronary artery beyond the obstruction. An artery, mammary or radial, is the first choice.

B.io: Compare and contrast precipitating factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis (including role of B-type natriuretic peptide, BNP), and treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
B.q: A 62-year-old woman is three days out from a myocardial infarction complicated by acute heart failure, with an ejection fraction of 30%. A colleague proposes an implantable defibrillator before discharge. Which step is premature at this point?
opts: Referring to cardiac rehabilitation
Cardiac rehabilitation is part of the pathway now. What is premature is the implantable device.
Optimizing her guideline therapy
Optimizing therapy is part of the pathway now. What is premature is the implantable device.
Starting a wearable defibrillator
The wearable defibrillator is exactly the first step for her. What is premature is the implantable device.
Implanting a defibrillator now

Correct. After acute heart failure from infarction, the pathway is a wearable defibrillator, optimized therapy and cardiac rehabilitation, then a repeat echocardiogram; the implantable device follows only if there is no improvement.
