C.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education, and prognosis
C.q: A 58-year-old woman with fatigue, cold intolerance and constipation is found to have blood pressure of 146/96 with a predominantly diastolic elevation. Which mechanism fits?
opts: Hyperthyroidism raising cardiac output
That produces a predominantly SYSTOLIC elevation with tachycardia, and her symptoms point the other way.
Hypothyroidism raising vascular resistance
Correct. Hypothyroidism raises systemic vascular resistance, which lifts the diastolic pressure, whereas hyperthyroidism raises cardiac output and lifts the systolic.
Autonomous aldosterone secretion
Aldosteronism produces resistant hypertension with hypokalemia rather than cold intolerance and constipation.
Catecholamine excess from an adrenal tumor
Pheochromocytoma causes paroxysmal symptoms rather than the sustained hypothyroid picture described.

C.io: Compare and contrast precipitating factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis (including role of B-type natriuretic peptide, BNP), and treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
C.q: A 78-year-old man was treated in the intensive care unit with dobutamine for acute heart failure. His daughter asks whether he can continue it at home to keep his heart strong. What is the most appropriate response?
opts: Only if his blood pressure is high
Blood pressure does not make dobutamine a home drug. Inotropes are for intensive care use only.
Yes, in place of his other medicines
Inotropes do not replace guideline-directed therapy and are for intensive care use only.
Inotropes are for intensive care only

Correct. Inotropic therapy, including dobutamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine and milrinone, is for intensive care use only. Outpatient therapy is guideline-directed therapy for his ejection fraction group.
Yes, as long-term home maintenance
Dobutamine is not a home maintenance therapy; inotropes are for intensive care use only.

C.io: Tricuspid stenosis
C.q: A 42-year-old woman has tricuspid stenosis seen on an echocardiogram and mild leg swelling. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Cardiology referral
Correct. Tricuspid stenosis is referred when it is seen on an echocardiogram or when there are heart failure related symptoms, both of which she has.
No follow-up needed
Tricuspid stenosis on an echocardiogram with heart failure related symptoms is referred to cardiology rather than dismissed.
Balloon valvotomy now
Balloon valvotomy is reserved for hepatic congestion or severe venous congestion. Tricuspid stenosis seen on echo is first referred to cardiology.
Mechanical replacement
Replacement is for severe symptomatic disease, and when done, a bioprosthetic valve is preferred. The first step for her is cardiology referral.

C.io: Pulmonic stenosis
C.q: What treatment does mild to moderate pulmonic stenosis need?
opts: None
Correct. Mild to moderate pulmonic stenosis needs no treatment and carries a 94% 20-year survival. Severe symptomatic disease is treated with diuretics and pulmonic balloon valvuloplasty.
A loop diuretic
Diuretics are for symptomatic right heart failure in severe pulmonic stenosis. Mild to moderate disease needs no treatment.
Balloon valvuloplasty
Pulmonic balloon valvuloplasty is for severe pulmonic stenosis with symptoms. Mild to moderate disease needs none.
Valve replacement
Replacement may be needed for severe congenital disease. Mild to moderate pulmonic stenosis needs no treatment.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
C.q: Which set of findings reflects inadequate tissue perfusion in heart failure?
opts: Tachycardia, a third heart sound and neck veins
Those reflect compensation, dilated-ventricle filling and congestion. Poor perfusion shows as fatigue, near-syncope and obtundation.
Hepatomegaly, nausea and ascites
Those reflect portal overload in right-sided failure. Poor perfusion shows as fatigue, near-syncope and obtundation.
Fatigue, near-syncope and obtundation
Correct. Inadequate tissue perfusion shows as weakness, fatigue, lethargy, malaise, syncope or near-syncope and obtundation, alongside renal dysfunction.
Orthopnea, crackles and edema
Those reflect congestion, the volume overload side of the syndrome. Poor perfusion shows as fatigue, near-syncope and obtundation.

C.io: Aortic stenosis
C.q: Which description fits the aortic stenosis murmur?
opts: Blowing holosystolic, to the axilla
A holosystolic blowing murmur radiating to the axilla is mitral regurgitation, heard at the apex. Aortic stenosis is harsh, ejection-type and radiates to the carotids.
Blowing early diastolic, to the apex
A high-pitched blowing diastolic murmur radiating to the apex is aortic regurgitation. Stenosis is harsh and systolic, and it radiates to the carotids.
Low diastolic rumble after a snap
A low-pitched diastolic rumble after an opening snap is mitral stenosis at the apex. Aortic stenosis is a harsh systolic ejection murmur.
Harsh systolic ejection, to the carotids
Correct. Aortic stenosis gives a harsh, systolic, crescendo-decrescendo ejection murmur at the second right intercostal space (right upper sternal border) that radiates to the carotids.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
C.q: A 79-year-old man with Parkinson disease faints when he gets up at night. His readings show a postural fall with a minimal heart rate rise. Which counseling point is most appropriate?
opts: Cut fluids to avoid night trips
Reducing fluid lowers volume and worsens postural falls; it is not listed advice for orthostatic syncope.
Stop all activity for a month
Inactivity is not a listed treatment; the advice targets how he changes position, alongside treating the cause.
Leap up to trigger his reflexes
Abrupt standing is what provokes the fall; with autonomic failure the reflex cannot compensate, so slow change is the advice.
Sit first, then stand up slowly
Correct. Slow positional changes are listed treatment for orthostatic syncope, and understanding why helps him follow the advice.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
C.q: A 38-year-old woman with very heavy menstrual bleeding has fatigue, palpitations, ankle edema and a raised B-type natriuretic peptide. Echocardiogram is being arranged. Which additional test is most likely to identify the driver of her heart failure?
opts: Complete blood count
Correct. Anemia is one of the causes of high-output failure, and the complete blood count is part of the high-output workup with the echocardiogram, metabolic panel and natriuretic peptide.
Chest radiograph
A radiograph can show congestion but not its cause. The complete blood count identifies anemia, the likely driver of high-output failure.
Right heart catheterization
Catheterization grades hemodynamic severity in right-sided failure. The complete blood count identifies anemia, the likely driver here.
Cardiac troponin level
Troponin looks for infarction or ischemic cardiomyopathy, which nothing here suggests. The complete blood count looks for the anemia that heavy bleeding causes.

C.topic: Chest pain workup and risk scores
C.io: Acute coronary syndrome
C.q: A 54-year-old man arrives at the emergency department with 30 minutes of chest pressure. Which pair of studies does every patient with chest pain receive?
opts: Calcium score and a lipid panel
A calcium score is for risk stratification, not acute chest pain, and lipids can come later. The universal first pair is a stat electrocardiogram and a chest radiograph.
Coronary angiography and echocardiogram
Coronary angiography is the gold standard for coronary disease but not the universal first study. Every chest pain patient starts with a stat electrocardiogram and a chest radiograph.
Treadmill stress test and D-dimer
A D-dimer is only a maybe in the chest pain workup, and a stress test is not done on arrival with active pain. Every patient gets a stat electrocardiogram and a chest radiograph.
Electrocardiogram and chest radiograph
Correct. All chest pain patients get a chest radiograph and a stat electrocardiogram. Blood work (complete blood count, metabolic panel, coagulation studies, troponin) follows.

C.io: Aortic regurgitation
C.q: A 60-year-old man with aortic insufficiency has an echocardiogram showing a regurgitant fraction of 62%. Which severity does this indicate?
opts: Mild regurgitation
Mild aortic regurgitation is a regurgitant fraction below 30%. A fraction of 62% is well into the severe range of 50% or more.
Moderate regurgitation
Moderate aortic regurgitation is a regurgitant fraction of 30 to 49%. At 62%, more than half the output is returning, which is severe.
Severe regurgitation
Correct. Aortic regurgitation is severe when 50% or more of the blood that passed the valve comes back. A fraction of 30 to 49% is moderate and below 30% is mild.
Ungradeable by echocardiogram
Regurgitant fraction is exactly how echocardiography grades aortic regurgitation; catheterization is definitive but not necessary. A fraction of 62% is severe.

C.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
C.q: Which warning features suggest renovascular disease?
opts: Weak or delayed femoral pulses
Delayed femoral pulses alongside upper limb hypertension suggest coarctation of the aorta rather than renal artery stenosis.
Proximal muscle weakness and broad purple striae
These are clues to Cushing syndrome, in which glucocorticoid excess promotes sodium retention and vasopressor sensitivity.
An abdominal bruit with asymmetric kidneys

Correct. Flash pulmonary edema is the one most easily missed, and it is also one of the features that most strongly argues for revascularization rather than medical management alone. Resistant or abrupt elevation and recurrent flash pulmonary edema are the other warning features.
Episodic headache, sweating and palpitations
This cluster suggests pheochromocytoma, where catecholamine excess produces paroxysmal symptoms alongside the hypertension.

C.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
C.q: A 73-year-old man has a faint while urinating at night, with nausea and sweating beforehand and quick recovery. Which test is used to exclude a cardiac dysrhythmia?
opts: A tilt-table test
Tilt-table testing is for postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome and does not show the cardiac rhythm.
A blood glucose level
A blood glucose excludes hypoglycemia, a non-hypotensive cause, rather than a dysrhythmia.
Orthostatic vital signs
Orthostatic readings look for a postural pressure fall; the rhythm is assessed with an electrocardiogram.
An electrocardiogram
Correct. A normal electrocardiogram lowers suspicion of a dysrhythmia, just as a normal glucose excludes hypoglycemia and blood tests address infection.

C.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education, and prognosis
C.q: A 54-year-old arrives late for a routine visit, is taken straight to the room and has her blood pressure measured immediately while she describes her morning. The cuff is placed over her sleeve and her legs are crossed. The reading is 152/94. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Reassure her that a single elevated reading is meaningless
It is not meaningless; it needs repeating under proper conditions. At least two readings are obtained, with any deviation from standard technique documented.
Diagnose stage 2 hypertension and start two agents
Two complementary agents are reasonable when pressure is substantially above goal, but not on a single reading taken outside standard conditions.
Order plasma metanephrines to exclude pheochromocytoma
Metanephrines are ordered when the history suggests episodic headache, sweating and palpitations, not because one office reading was high.
Repeat it after five minutes of quiet rest

Correct. Every departure here inflates the reading: no rest period, talking during the measurement, a sleeved arm and crossed legs. A diagnosis rests on readings taken to standard, and acting on this one would start treatment on an artifact. Correct technique matters as much as the rest period.

C.io: Compare and contrast anticoagulation therapy for prosthetic heart valves.
C.q: A 58-year-old woman with a mechanical mitral valve asks whether she could take daily aspirin instead of her current anticoagulant. Which long-term therapy is recommended for her?
opts: A vitamin K antagonist
Correct. With a mechanical heart valve, vitamin K antagonist therapy is recommended over no vitamin K antagonist and over antiplatelet agents. Warfarin is the one most commonly used.
Aspirin in place of it
Antiplatelet agents are specifically ranked below vitamin K antagonist therapy for a mechanical valve. Aspirin cannot replace her anticoagulant.
No drug after one year
A mechanical valve requires lifelong anticoagulation; it is biological valves that stop after the postoperative period. She stays on a vitamin K antagonist.
Heparin every day
Heparin bridges gaps in warfarin around surgery; it is not the long-term therapy. The recommendation is a vitamin K antagonist.

C.io: Compare and contrast precipitating factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis (including role of B-type natriuretic peptide, BNP), and treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
C.q: A 60-year-old woman wore a defibrillator vest for three months after an infarction, with optimized guideline-directed therapy and cardiac rehabilitation. Her repeat echocardiogram shows an ejection fraction of 28%. She is class II and expected to live many years. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Continue the vest indefinitely
The vest bridges the recovery period. With no improvement on the repeat echocardiogram, the next step is an implantable defibrillator.
Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator

Correct. The pathway ends with an implantable device when the repeat echocardiogram shows no improvement. She also meets the criteria: ejection fraction 35% or less, class II or III, optimal therapy and life expectancy of at least one year.
Stop therapy and recheck in a year
Stopping therapy would undo the optimization. With no improvement, the next step is an implantable defibrillator.
Heart transplant evaluation now
Transplant is reserved for failure that cannot be controlled. She is class II and meets the criteria for an implantable defibrillator.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
C.q: A 73-year-old woman with neurogenic orthostatic hypotension from diabetes also has chronic kidney disease. She remains symptomatic despite slow position changes. Which treatment should be avoided?
opts: Midodrine
Correct. Chronic kidney disease is one of the listed settings, with supine hypertension and severe heart disease, in which midodrine is avoided.
Droxidopa
Droxidopa is a mild adjunct that is better with supine hypertension; kidney disease is not a reason given to avoid it.
Slow position changes
Slow positional changes remain first-line for orthostatic syncope and are safe with kidney disease.
Fludrocortisone
Fludrocortisone is avoided in heart failure because of salt and water retention; kidney disease is not its listed warning.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
C.q: A 60-year-old man is newly diagnosed with heart failure and will start a loop diuretic. Which laboratory panel should be checked before starting?
opts: Coagulation panel
Clotting tests are not the pre-diuretic check. Potassium and renal function come from the complete metabolic panel.
Complete metabolic panel
Correct. The metabolic panel gives potassium and renal function (blood urea nitrogen, creatinine and filtration rate), both of which a potassium-wasting loop diuretic affects.
Hepatic function panel
Liver tests are not what the diuretic calls for. Potassium and renal function come from the complete metabolic panel.
Thyroid function panel
Thyroid testing is not the pre-diuretic check. Potassium and renal function come from the complete metabolic panel.

C.io: Mitral valve prolapse
C.q: A 34-year-old woman with mitral valve prolapse has now developed symptomatic severe mitral regurgitation with a falling ejection fraction. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: A mitral clip or valve replacement
Correct. Prolapse usually needs no treatment, but if it progresses to mitral regurgitation the options are a clip, transcatheter mitral valve replacement, or biological or mechanical replacement.
Aortic valve replacement
Aortic valve replacement treats disease of the aortic valve. Prolapse that progresses to mitral regurgitation is treated at the mitral valve.
Percutaneous balloon valvotomy
Balloon valvotomy treats severe mitral stenosis. A prolapsed valve that now leaks severely is treated with a clip or replacement.
Reassurance with no treatment
Reassurance fits uncomplicated prolapse. Once it has progressed to symptomatic severe regurgitation, a clip or valve replacement is indicated.

C.io: Identify medical care strategies for coronary artery disease in the lecture topic list for the following populations.
C.q: A 38-year-old woman who smokes a pack of cigarettes a day asks whether smoking really matters for her heart at her age. Which counseling point is accurate?
opts: It matters only after menopause
Smoking is not a postmenopausal risk only. It is a strong predictor of coronary disease especially in women younger than 45, which is exactly her group.
It raises risk only in men
Smoking raises risk in both sexes and is a strong predictor especially in women younger than 45, so it matters for her now.
It is a strong predictor at her age
Correct. Smoking is a modifiable coronary risk factor and a strong predictor, especially in women younger than 45. Her age makes the counseling more urgent, not less.
It matters only with diabetes
Smoking is an independent modifiable risk factor; it does not need diabetes to count. It is a strong predictor especially in women younger than 45.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
C.q: A 69-year-old man reports lightheadedness and dimming vision within a minute or two of standing, which settles when he sits. His examination at rest is normal. Which test should be performed first?
opts: Orthostatic vital signs
Correct. Pressure and heart rate taken supine and again within 3 minutes of standing show whether orthostatic criteria are met and which type the heart rate response suggests.
An echocardiogram
Echocardiography evaluates structural cardiogenic syncope; symptoms that follow standing call first for a postural pressure measurement.
A tilt-table test
The tilt-table test is the listed test for postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, and its sensitivity of about 40% makes a negative result weak.
A stress test
A stress test belongs to the arrhythmia work-up of cardiogenic syncope, not the first test for a postural pattern of symptoms.

C.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
C.q: Which are the earliest measurable markers of hypertensive kidney damage?
opts: Hematuria and casts on urinalysis
Blood and casts on urinalysis point toward alternative renal causes requiring evaluation rather than serving as the earliest markers of hypertensive damage.
Rising albuminuria and falling filtration rate
Correct, and both are watched as trends rather than single values, because it is the direction of travel over time that identifies progression early enough to act on.
A rising serum potassium concentration
Potassium is measured to screen for aldosteronism and before starting therapy rather than as an early marker of hypertensive renal injury.
A further rise in the blood pressure itself
The pressure is the cause under investigation; albuminuria and falling filtration are what measure the damage it has done.

C.io: Define the following diagnostic and therapeutic groups of HF patients, and the treatment implications/recommendations for each group: a. HF with reduced EF (HFrEF) b. HF with mildly reduced EF (HFmrEF) c. HF with preserved EF (HFpEF)
C.q: A 62-year-old woman is newly diagnosed with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (fraction 28%). She is breathless with ordinary exertion but comfortable at rest, and takes no renin-angiotensin drug. Which agent fits her symptom class?
opts: Dobutamine
Dobutamine is an inotrope for intensive care use only. Her class II reduced ejection fraction fits sacubitril-valsartan.
Metolazone alone
Metolazone is a thiazide-like diuretic used as needed for congestion, not renin-angiotensin therapy. Her class fits sacubitril-valsartan.
Sacubitril-valsartan
Correct. Symptoms with exertion are New York Heart Association class II, and the angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor is recommended for class II to III in reduced ejection fraction.
Diltiazem
Diltiazem is a calcium channel blocker, which is avoided in heart failure. Her class II reduced ejection fraction fits sacubitril-valsartan.

C.topic: ST-elevation infarction and right ventricular infarct
C.io: ST segment elevation
C.q: A 66-year-old man is admitted with an inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction that extends into the right ventricle, with ST elevation in the right-sided lead V4R. His daughter asks why he is not being given nitroglycerin for his chest pain. What should she be told?
opts: It would slow his heart rate
Slowing the heart rate is the concern with a beta blocker, which is withheld for bradycardia. Nitroglycerin is withheld because it lowers the preload his failing right ventricle needs.
It would lower his preload

Correct. In a right ventricular infarct, nitroglycerin is not given: decreasing the preload reduces the Frank-Starling effect on the right ventricle, which can fail into right-sided heart failure, dropping output and precipitating shock.
It would cause bleeding
Bleeding, including intracerebral hemorrhage, is the risk of thrombolytics, not nitroglycerin. Nitroglycerin is withheld because it lowers the preload his right ventricle depends on.
It would cause coronary spasm
Nitroglycerin relieves coronary spasm rather than causing it, and response to it is part of diagnosing vasospastic angina. Here it is withheld because lowering preload can drop his output into shock.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atherosclerosis and lipid disorders: 1. Hypertriglyceridemia 2. Hypercholesterolemia 3. HDL cholesterol 4. LDL and VLDL cholesterol
C.q: Which lipoprotein consists mostly of cholesterol and supplies cholesterol for cellular needs?
opts: Low-density lipoprotein

Correct. Low-density lipoprotein consists mostly of cholesterol, is used to provide cholesterol for cellular needs, and its increased levels put patients at risk for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.
Chylomicrons
Chylomicrons carry dietary triglyceride after a fatty meal and are the least dense class.
Very-low-density lipoprotein
Very-low-density lipoprotein consists mainly of triglyceride with some cholesterol and transfers triglycerides to the cells.
High-density lipoprotein
High-density lipoprotein carries excess cholesterol away from the periphery to the liver, the reverse direction.

C.io: Mitral regurgitation
C.q: A 59-year-old man has a holosystolic blowing murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla. He is asked to squeeze a hand grip firmly for a minute while the examiner listens. How does the murmur change?
opts: It becomes diastolic
No maneuver moves a murmur from systole into diastole; mitral regurgitation stays holosystolic. Handgrip simply makes it louder.
It does not change
Handgrip does change it: raising peripheral resistance to ejection augments regurgitation into the left atrium, so the murmur gets louder.
It becomes louder
Correct. Squatting and handgrip increase the mitral regurgitation murmur: peripheral vascular resistance to ventricular ejection rises and pushes more regurgitation back into the left atrium.
It becomes softer
Softening is the response of mitral regurgitation to standing or the Valsalva maneuver. Handgrip raises resistance to ejection and makes the murmur louder.

C.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education, and prognosis
C.q: A 64-year-old hypertensive man also has a raised low-density lipoprotein. What principle should guide his management?
opts: Treat the lipids first and defer blood pressure control
Neither is deferred; total cardiovascular risk is addressed, since both drive the same vascular injury.
Treat total cardiovascular risk, not pressure alone

Correct. Hypertension accelerates atherosclerosis through shear stress, intimal injury, lipid oxidation and smooth muscle proliferation, so antiplatelet and lipid-lowering therapy are considered where indicated.
Lipid therapy is unnecessary once blood pressure reaches goal
Reaching the pressure goal does not remove the contribution of lipids to the same process.
Treat the blood pressure and address lipids only if it fails
The two are managed together, because the vascular injury they produce is a single process.

C.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
C.q: A 74-year-old man with a prior heart attack and reduced ejection fraction collapsed abruptly while walking, with no warning except a brief racing heartbeat. He is pale, his pressure is 86/52 and his heart rate is 150 and regular. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Vasovagal reflex syncope
Vasovagal syncope follows triggers such as fear or heat with a warm, nauseated prodrome and a slow rather than fast heart rate.
Non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
Non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension follows standing, often with volume loss; he collapsed abruptly mid-walk after palpitations.
Situational reflex syncope
Situational syncope follows a bodily function such as urination, with a reflex prodrome and quick recovery.
Cardiogenic syncope from an arrhythmia

Correct. Abrupt collapse with minimal prodrome after palpitations, in a patient with coronary disease and reduced ejection fraction, with a rapid regular rhythm, points to an arrhythmic cardiac cause.

C.io: Compare and contrast precipitating factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis (including role of B-type natriuretic peptide, BNP), and treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
C.q: A 70-year-old man admitted with acute heart failure has diuresed well. On the day of planned discharge his B-type natriuretic peptide is 360. What does this predischarge level suggest?
opts: Acute heart failure is still likely
Acute failure becomes likely above 900. A predischarge level of 360 is below 430 and linked to lower readmission.
Higher risk of 30-day readmission
Risk rises with higher levels. Below 430 predischarge, the readmission risk is lower.
Lower risk of 30-day readmission
Correct. A predischarge level below 430 carries a lower risk of readmission within 30 days, which supports discharge planning.
The level carries no prognostic value
Predischarge levels do carry prognostic meaning: below 430 is linked to lower 30-day readmission.

C.io: Differentiate between systolic dysfunction and diastolic dysfunction..
C.q: A 64-year-old man with a myocardial infarction three years ago has breathlessness on exertion and orthopnea (breathlessness lying flat). Blood pressure is 104/68. There is a third heart sound (an extra sound in early diastole just after the second heart sound) and bibasilar crackles. B-type natriuretic peptide is 820. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Diastolic failure from hypertrophic disease
The diastolic chain runs with hypertension, a fourth heart sound and edema that starts peripherally. His low pressure, third sound and prior infarction point to systolic failure.
Isolated right-sided failure from the lungs
Right-sided failure shows peripheral edema, distended neck veins and portal overload. Crackles, orthopnea and a third sound point to left-sided systolic failure.
Systolic failure from ischemic cardiomyopathy

Correct. Every link of the systolic chain is here: ischemic cardiomyopathy after infarction, a low-normal blood pressure, a third heart sound from rapid filling of a dilated ventricle, and pulmonary edema, confirmed by an elevated natriuretic peptide.
High-output failure from increased demand
High-output failure comes from anemia, hyperthyroidism or an arteriovenous fistula, with no infarction behind it. This is systolic failure from ischemic cardiomyopathy.

C.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education, and prognosis
C.q: A 57-year-old woman with a hypertensive emergency has her pressure reduced from 240/130 to 125/75 within thirty minutes. She then develops a new hemiparesis. What happened?
opts: Hyperkalemia precipitated the event
Potassium disturbance relates to renin-angiotensin blockade rather than to the rate of pressure reduction.
She developed rebound hypertension
Rebound on abrupt withdrawal is a limitation of central alpha-2 agonists and does not explain a deficit after an over-rapid reduction.
The reduction was appropriate and the deficit is unrelated
Reducing to a chronic goal within the first hour is specifically capable of causing ischemic stroke, myocardial injury or renal failure.
Autoregulation had adapted to the higher pressure

Correct. Her organs had reset the range over which they protect their own perfusion, so a value that would be safe in anyone else left her brain underperfused. Reducing it that fast left her brain underperfused.

C.io: Non-ST segment elevation
C.q: A 68-year-old woman has an hour of substernal pressure. Her electrocardiogram shows ST-segment depression of 2 mm in V5 and V6 without ST elevation, and her standard troponin I is 0.62 ng/mL. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Infarction with ST elevation
An ST-elevation infarction needs ST elevation above 1 mm in two or more leads. Her tracing shows ST depression with no elevation, so the infarct is non-ST-elevation.
Vasospastic angina
Vasospastic angina causes transient ST changes during an episode of rest pain that resolve, with normal coronaries at angiography. It does not explain an hour of pain with an elevated troponin I.
Unstable angina
Unstable angina has the same kind of electrocardiogram changes but a troponin I that is not abnormal. Her troponin I of 0.62 ng/mL is elevated, which makes it an infarction.
Infarction without ST elevation

Correct. ST-segment depression above 1 mm and/or T-wave inversion in two or more consecutive leads, with symptoms and an elevated troponin I (standard troponin I above 0.04 ng/mL), is a non-ST-elevation infarction.

C.io: Mitral stenosis
C.q: A 39-year-old woman who emigrated from a country where rheumatic fever is common has breathlessness on exertion and orthopnea (breathlessness lying flat). A diastolic rumble is heard at the apex. Which is the most appropriate initial test?
opts: Electrocardiogram only
An electrocardiogram may show left atrial abnormality or atrial fibrillation, but it does not show the valve. Suggestive symptoms call for an echocardiogram.
No test until symptoms worsen
She already has suggestive symptoms, and dyspnea on exertion or orthopnea is the trigger for an echocardiogram. Waiting would miss a treatable stenosis.
Cardiac catheterization
Cardiac catheterization is not necessary for mitral stenosis and is usually done for an ischemic evaluation. The test that answers her symptoms is a transthoracic echocardiogram.
Transthoracic echocardiogram
Correct. Any patient with symptoms suggestive of mitral stenosis, such as dyspnea on exertion or orthopnea, should get an echocardiogram. It shows a large left atrium and the stenotic mitral valve.

D.io: Acute coronary syndrome
D.q: A 57-year-old man had a drug-eluting stent placed two weeks ago for an acute coronary syndrome. He tells you the clopidogrel is expensive and he plans to stop it because his chest pain is gone. What should he be told?
opts: Aspirin alone now protects the stent
After a stent, protection comes from dual antiplatelet therapy: clopidogrel plus aspirin together. Dropping clopidogrel in the first 6 weeks is the strongest predictor of sudden stent thrombosis.
Missed doses matter only if pain returns
Stent thrombosis can come suddenly and without warning. Missing dual antiplatelet therapy in the first 6 weeks after a stent is the strongest predictor of it.
Stopping now risks a clot in the stent

Correct. Stopping dual antiplatelet therapy (a P2Y12 receptor antagonist such as clopidogrel plus aspirin) in the first 6 weeks after a stent is the strongest predictor of stent thrombosis, a sudden clot that occludes the stent and can cause a large, often fatal infarction.
It can stop once the chest pain is gone
The medication protects the stent, not the symptom. Stopping dual antiplatelet therapy in the first 6 weeks risks sudden stent thrombosis, pain or no pain.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atherosclerosis and lipid disorders: 1. Hypertriglyceridemia 2. Hypercholesterolemia 3. HDL cholesterol 4. LDL and VLDL cholesterol
D.q: Which two lipoproteins are the main transporters of triglycerides?
opts: High-density lipoprotein and chylomicrons
Chylomicrons do carry triglyceride, but high-density lipoprotein carries cholesterol back to the liver, so the pair is half wrong.
Low-density lipoprotein and lipoprotein(a)
Both are cholesterol-rich particles built on apolipoprotein B-100; neither is a main triglyceride carrier.
Chylomicrons and very-low-density lipoprotein
Correct. Triglyceride transport belongs to chylomicrons (dietary fat) and very-low-density lipoprotein (made by the liver); cholesterol transport belongs to the low- and high-density classes.
Low- and high-density lipoprotein
These two are the cholesterol transporters, the 'bad' and 'good' cholesterol respectively, rather than the carriers of triglyceride.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
D.q: A 61-year-old woman has had left-sided heart failure with reduced ejection fraction for five years. Over two months she has developed leg edema, jugular venous distension (distended neck veins), an enlarged liver, nausea and poor appetite. Which is the most likely explanation for her new findings?
opts: High-output failure from increased demand
High-output failure comes from anemia, hyperthyroidism or an arteriovenous fistula. Her picture is right-sided failure following chronic left-sided disease.
Worsening systolic failure of the left only
Left-sided worsening would add orthopnea and crackles. Edema, neck veins and portal congestion mean the right ventricle has now failed.
Primary liver disease with ascites
The enlarged liver here is congestion from right ventricular failure, which also explains her distended neck veins and edema.
Right-sided failure from her left-sided failure

Correct. Chronic left-sided failure is the most common cause of right-sided failure. Systemic overload gives edema and distended neck veins; portal overload gives nausea, poor appetite and hepatomegaly.

D.io: Aortic regurgitation
D.q: A 34-year-old man with Marfan syndrome has a high-pitched blowing diastolic murmur at the third intercostal space at the left upper sternal border that radiates to the apex. He has bounding pulses and a wide pulse pressure. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Aortic regurgitation

Correct. Blowing means regurgitation and diastolic narrows it to the aortic or pulmonic valve; the third intercostal space with radiation to the apex, bounding pulses and a wide pulse pressure mark aortic regurgitation. Marfan syndrome is a root-disease cause.
Mitral regurgitation
Mitral regurgitation is blowing but holosystolic, at the apex, radiating to the axilla. This murmur is diastolic, which points to the aortic valve.
Pulmonic regurgitation
Pulmonic regurgitation is a brief early diastolic murmur at the second left intercostal space that radiates toward the right sternal border. It does not produce bounding pulses.
Mitral stenosis
Mitral stenosis is diastolic too, but it is a low-pitched rumble at the apex that starts with an opening snap. Rumble means stenosis; this murmur is blowing.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
D.q: Which drug class is recommended to prevent heart failure in patients with diabetes who have no structural heart disease?
opts: Beta blocker started at diagnosis
A beta blocker is not part of stage A prevention; it is a stage B therapy once structural disease appears. Prevention in diabetes uses a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
Hydralazine with isosorbide dinitrate
This pairing is reserved for African American patients with reduced ejection fraction in functional class III or IV. Stage A prevention uses a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
Angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor
This combination belongs to symptomatic reduced ejection fraction in functional class II or III. Stage A prevention in diabetes uses a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor

Correct. Prevention in stage A, risk factors with a normal heart, carries one strong drug recommendation: a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor for patients with diabetes, ahead of any beta blocker, which is a stage B therapy.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
D.q: A 70-year-old man on a newly increased diuretic keeps standing up quickly despite advice, and his pressure falls 30 mmHg on standing. If this continues, what is he most at risk of?
opts: Diabetic autonomic neuropathy
Autonomic neuropathy arises from long-standing diabetes, not from a medication-related fall in pressure.
Syncope from cerebral hypoperfusion
Correct. Syncope is the result of symptomatic hypotension: when the standing pressure falls far enough, brain perfusion drops and consciousness is briefly lost.
A seizure disorder
Seizure is a separate, non-hypotensive cause of loss of consciousness, not a consequence of orthostatic hypotension.
Supine hypertension overnight
Supine hypertension is high pressure while lying flat, a comorbidity that changes the criterion, not a consequence of a diuretic-related fall.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
D.q: A 64-year-old man with reduced ejection fraction (fraction 30%) on sacubitril-valsartan, a beta blocker, spironolactone and empagliflozin develops atrial fibrillation, and rate control is being planned. Which medication should be avoided?
opts: Sacubitril-valsartan
Sacubitril-valsartan is recommended in reduced ejection fraction for class II to III. The drug to avoid is diltiazem.
Spironolactone
Spironolactone is a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, a strong recommendation in reduced ejection fraction. The drug to avoid is diltiazem.
Empagliflozin
Empagliflozin is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor, part of core therapy in reduced ejection fraction. The drug to avoid is diltiazem.
Diltiazem
Correct. Diltiazem is a calcium channel blocker, and calcium channel blockers are avoided in heart failure. His existing beta blocker belongs to core therapy.

D.io: Compare and contrast precipitating factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis (including role of B-type natriuretic peptide, BNP), and treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
D.q: A 73-year-old woman with chronic heart failure has a B-type natriuretic peptide that has risen by 100 since her last visit. What does this change imply?
opts: About 90% higher relative risk of death
That overstates it. Each rise of 100 carries about a 35% increase in the relative risk of death.
No change in her relative risk of death
The level carries prognostic weight: each rise of 100 adds about 35% to the relative risk of death.
About 5% higher relative risk of death
That understates it. Each rise of 100 carries about a 35% increase in the relative risk of death.
About 35% higher relative risk of death
Correct. Each increase of 100 carries about a 35% increase in the relative risk of death, so a rising level is a warning sign even when symptoms seem stable.

D.io: Mitral regurgitation
D.q: Mitral regurgitation is backflow into which chamber?
opts: The right ventricle, in diastole
Backflow into the right ventricle during diastole is pulmonic regurgitation. Mitral regurgitation leaks into the left atrium during systole.
The left atrium, in systole

Correct. Mitral regurgitation is incomplete closure of the mitral valve, so blood flows back into the left atrium while the ventricle contracts, leading to left atrial dilation with pressure and volume overload.
The left ventricle, in diastole
Backflow into the left ventricle during diastole is aortic regurgitation. Mitral regurgitation leaks into the left atrium during systole.
The right atrium, in systole
Backflow from the right ventricle into the right atrium during systole is tricuspid regurgitation. Mitral regurgitation leaks into the left atrium.

D.io: Define the following diagnostic and therapeutic groups of HF patients, and the treatment implications/recommendations for each group: a. HF with reduced EF (HFrEF) b. HF with mildly reduced EF (HFmrEF) c. HF with preserved EF (HFpEF)
D.q: A 74-year-old woman with long-standing hypertension has leg edema, crackles and breathlessness climbing stairs. Echocardiogram shows an ejection fraction of 62% and B-type natriuretic peptide is 640. Which therapy carries the strongest recommendation now?
opts: An inotrope such as dobutamine
Inotropes are for intensive care use only. With preserved fraction and congestion, the strong recommendation is a diuretic as needed.
Hydralazine with isosorbide dinitrate
That pairing is for African American patients with reduced ejection fraction in functional class III or IV. With preserved fraction and congestion, the strong recommendation is a diuretic.
A diuretic as needed for congestion

Correct. With preserved ejection fraction and congestion, diuretics as needed carry the strong recommendation. A sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor is next at moderate strength; the neprilysin combination, antagonist and receptor blocker are weak.
A beta blocker titrated to heart rate
A beta blocker is core therapy in reduced ejection fraction, not the strongest recommendation with a preserved fraction. Her congestion is treated with a diuretic as needed.

D.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
D.q: A 70-year-old man fainted at home and has recovered. His electrocardiogram and glucose are normal. Which tests look for an infectious or metabolic contributor?
opts: A blood count and metabolic panel
Correct. Unremarkable blood counts and a metabolic panel lower suspicion of an infectious or metabolic source, as glucose and the electrocardiogram address hypoglycemia and dysrhythmia.
A tilt-table test and a log
A tilt-table test belongs to the tachycardia syndrome and a log to reflex syncope; neither screens for infection.
Orthostatic vitals only
Orthostatic readings test for a postural fall and cannot detect an infectious or metabolic source.
An echocardiogram and stress test
These evaluate structural and arrhythmic cardiac causes rather than infection or metabolic disturbance.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
D.q: A 71-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy has an ejection fraction of 25%, is class II on optimal guideline-directed therapy, and has metastatic cancer with an expected survival of a few months. Which is most appropriate regarding an implantable defibrillator?
opts: Implant it before discharge
His fraction and class qualify, but the life expectancy criterion of at least one year does not. The device is not indicated.
Implant it once he is class IV
Class IV falls outside the class II to III criterion, and his life expectancy still fails. The device is not indicated.
Implant it after a cardiac arrest
The criteria do not wait for an arrest, and his life expectancy of months fails them. The device is not indicated.
It is not indicated for him

Correct. The device is indicated only with a life expectancy of at least one year, together with ejection fraction 35% or less, class II or III and optimal therapy. His expected survival of months fails that criterion.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
D.q: Which condition is associated with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome?
opts: Multiple system atrophy
Multiple system atrophy causes neurogenic orthostatic hypotension through autonomic failure, not the tachycardia syndrome.
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
Correct. Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is the association given for the syndrome, which mostly affects women aged 15 to 50.
Long-standing diabetes
Long-standing diabetes with neuropathy causes diabetic autonomic neuropathy and neurogenic orthostatic hypotension.
Parkinson disease
Parkinson disease is an example cause of neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, where the heart rate rises only minimally.

D.q: A 38-year-old man has an average home blood pressure of 126/78. He has no diabetes, no kidney disease and no cardiovascular history. What should he be advised?
opts: Lifestyle treatment

Correct. An elevated reading that does not yet warrant medication still warrants an intervention, and lifestyle measures continue alongside drugs later rather than being replaced by them. It is recommended at every blood pressure category.
Start a thiazide-type diuretic now
Medication is not indicated at this reading, and lifestyle measures apply first and throughout.
No intervention is needed until he reaches stage 1
Lifestyle treatment is recommended for every category, including readings below the threshold for medication.
Recheck in five years with no advice in the interim
That defers an intervention recommended at every blood pressure category, including this one.

D.q: A 72-year-old woman with heart failure asks why she must take several medicines when she already feels better. Which explanation matches the goals of treatment?
opts: They are meant to cure her cardiomyopathy
Cure is not among the treatment goals. The goals are fewer symptoms, longer survival and slower progression.
They are meant to make her ejection fraction normal
A normal ejection fraction is not a goal of treatment. The goals are fewer symptoms, longer survival and slower progression.
They are only needed while she has symptoms
Symptom relief is one goal among three. Increasing survival and limiting progression continue after she feels better.
They also extend life and slow progression
Correct. The goals are to decrease symptoms, increase survival and limit disease progression. Feeling better meets only the first of the three, so the regimen continues.

D.q: A 49-year-old newly diagnosed hypertensive patient has fundoscopy showing generalized arteriolar narrowing and arteriovenous nicking, with no hemorrhages or exudates. What does this tell you?
opts: These findings carry no prognostic weight
Hypertensive retinopathy predicts long-term stroke risk independently of the blood pressure level.
They reflect current and previous pressure
Correct. Generalized narrowing and nicking record the accumulated burden, whereas focal narrowing, hemorrhages and exudates relate to CURRENT pressure only.
These findings indicate a hypertensive emergency
Optic disc edema marks acute hypertensive injury; chronic arteriolar changes do not.
These changes reflect current blood pressure only
Focal narrowing, hemorrhages and exudates are the findings tied to current pressure; these two relate to current and previous.

D.io: Tricuspid regurgitation
D.q: A 58-year-old woman with a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that increases with inspiration is examined further. Which additional finding is most expected?
opts: A collapsing radial pulse
A collapsing, water hammer pulse is the Corrigan pulse of aortic regurgitation. Tricuspid regurgitation gives an elevated jugular venous pressure with neck pulsations.
Head bobbing with each beat
Head bobbing is the de Musset sign of aortic regurgitation. Tricuspid regurgitation gives elevated jugular pulsations and a venous thrill.
Delayed, weak carotid pulse
A delayed, weakened carotid with a forceful apex is the clue to severe aortic stenosis. Tricuspid regurgitation raises the jugular venous pressure.
Elevated jugular pulsations
Correct. Tricuspid regurgitation raises the jugular venous pressure with visible neck pulsations, and there may be a venous thrill (a palpable vibration) over the right jugular vein.

D.io: Pulmonic regurgitation
D.q: A 35-year-old man has a brief early diastolic murmur at the second left intercostal space from pulmonic regurgitation. Which maneuver makes the murmur louder?
opts: Squatting
Correct. Anything that increases venous return increases the pulmonic regurgitation murmur -- inspiration, squatting and lying supine. Expiration and standing decrease it.
Standing
Standing reduces venous return, so it softens the pulmonic regurgitation murmur. Squatting, inspiration and lying supine make it louder.
Sitting upright
Sitting up does not add venous return the way lying supine does. Squatting, inspiration and the supine position increase the murmur.
Expiration
Expiration reduces venous return to the right heart and softens right-sided murmurs. Inspiration, squatting and lying supine make it louder.

D.q: An 81-year-old woman has progressive breathlessness and ankle edema over three months. Her N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide is 720. What does this level suggest for her age?
opts: Only a younger cut-off applies
The age-specific threshold exists precisely for patients older than 75: above 450 heart failure is likely.
The level is normal for her age
The age-adjusted threshold over 75 is 450, and 720 exceeds it. Heart failure is likely.
Heart failure is ruled out
No rule-out applies at 720. Older than 75, a level above 450 makes heart failure likely.
Heart failure is likely
Correct. Older than 75, an N-terminal fragment above 450 makes heart failure likely. In a younger patient the threshold would be 125.

D.q: A 59-year-old hypertensive man is breathless with bibasal crackles and raised jugular venous pressure. Is chest radiography appropriate?
opts: Yes, as a routine part of every hypertensive workup
Routine chest radiography is specifically not indicated for uncomplicated hypertension.
No, because chest radiography is never indicated in hypertension
It is not indicated ROUTINELY for uncomplicated hypertension, which is different from never being indicated.
No, because a normal film would exclude dissection
A normal chest radiograph does not exclude dissection, so that is not a reason either way.
Yes, because findings suggest pulmonary edema
Correct. Radiography is appropriate when dyspnea or findings suggest pulmonary edema, when cardiomegaly is suspected, or when a widened mediastinum is a concern.

D.q: A 52-year-old man with low high-density lipoprotein has improved his lifestyle, and his clinician is weighing a drug chosen specifically to raise high-density lipoprotein. Which drug raises it most?
opts: Niacin
Correct. Niacin raises high-density lipoprotein 15% to 35%, better than other medications, compared with fibrates 10% to 30%, statins 5% to 22% and ezetimibe 8%.
Ezetimibe
Ezetimibe raises high-density lipoprotein only about 8% and is used mainly as a low-density adjunct.
Colesevelam
Colesevelam is a bile acid sequestrant that lowers low-density lipoprotein 15% to 30% as an adjunct and is not used to raise high-density lipoprotein.
Pravastatin
Statins such as pravastatin raise high-density lipoprotein 5% to 22%, less than niacin.

D.q: A 40-year-old man is newly found to have heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia with low-density lipoprotein of 250 mg/dL. He has read about a new injectable and wants it instead of any pill. Which option is inappropriate as initial therapy?
opts: A high-intensity statin
A high-intensity statin is the common first regimen in heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia and is entirely appropriate.
A low saturated-fat, low-cholesterol diet
A diet low in saturated fat and cholesterol is part of his treatment, alongside the statin, so it is appropriate.
Addressing smoking and blood pressure
Aggressive reduction of vascular risk factors such as smoking, hypertension and diabetes is recommended, so this is appropriate.
Evolocumab before trying a statin
Correct. The steps must be followed: high-intensity statins first, then ezetimibe and nicotinic acid, and the injectable only for patients refractory to drug therapy.

D.q: A 49-year-old man who drinks heavily is admitted for an unrelated procedure. On the second day his blood pressure rises sharply. What explains this?
opts: Moderate alcohol should be resumed for cardiovascular benefit
Starting or resuming alcohol for cardiovascular benefit is specifically not recommended; intake is limited to low-risk thresholds.
Alcohol lowers pressure, so stopping returns him to baseline
Excess alcohol raises rather than lowers blood pressure, so this reverses the relationship.
Alcohol withdrawal can produce acute severe hypertension
Correct, and the relationship runs both ways: excess alcohol raises blood pressure chronically, and withdrawal from it can raise it acutely.
Only chronic excess raises pressure; withdrawal has no effect
Withdrawal is specifically capable of producing acute severe hypertension, which is what is happening here.

D.q: A 59-year-old woman develops a persistent dry cough six weeks after starting lisinopril. Her blood pressure is at goal. What is the appropriate response?
opts: Stop all antihypertensive therapy
A tolerability problem with one agent is managed by substitution rather than by abandoning treatment.
Switch to an angiotensin receptor blocker
Correct. The cough is bradykinin-mediated and occurs in up to about one in five. Angiotensin receptor blockers do not raise bradykinin, so the effect is lost while the therapeutic action is kept.
Add an antitussive and continue the lisinopril
Switching class removes the mechanism rather than masking the symptom, and an equally effective alternative exists.
Add losartan to the lisinopril
Dual renin-angiotensin blockade is specifically prohibited because of hyperkalemia and kidney injury risk.

D.q: A 50-year-old woman has a waist circumference of 38 inches, triglyceride of 190 mg/dL, high-density lipoprotein of 45 mg/dL, blood pressure of 134/88 and fasting glucose of 104 mg/dL. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia
Dysbetalipoproteinemia raises triglyceride and total cholesterol together to 250 to 500 with palmar xanthomas.
Severe hypertriglyceridemia
The severe form requires triglyceride above 500 mg/dL; hers is 190, which is only borderline high.
Mixed dyslipidemia
Mixed dyslipidemia needs low-density lipoprotein above 130 or non-high-density above 160 with triglyceride above 150; her findings are the metabolic cluster.
Metabolic syndrome
Correct. Any three of five criteria establish it; she meets four: waist above 35 inches, triglyceride above 150, high-density lipoprotein below 50 in a woman and blood pressure above 130/85.

D.topic: ST-elevation infarction and right ventricular infarct
D.io: ST segment elevation
D.q: Nitroglycerin is withheld in a right ventricular infarct because the injured right ventricle depends on what?
opts: A slow heart rate
Bradycardia is the reason a beta blocker is withheld in an infarction, not a need of the right ventricle. Nitroglycerin is withheld because it removes the preload the right ventricle depends on.
Adequate preload

Correct. The infarcted right ventricle is preload dependent: nitroglycerin decreases preload, which reduces the Frank-Starling effect on its myocardium, so it fails into right-sided heart failure, output drops and shock follows.
Relief of spasm
Coronary spasm drives vasospastic angina, and nitroglycerin relieves it. A right ventricular infarct comes from right coronary artery occlusion, and its failing ventricle depends on preload.
Extra oxygen
Oxygen is given in an infarction only when the oxygen saturation is below 91%, and nitroglycerin does not take it away. Nitroglycerin lowers the preload the right ventricle depends on.

D.io: Differentiate between systolic dysfunction and diastolic dysfunction..
D.q: A 71-year-old woman with 20 years of poorly controlled hypertension has ankle swelling that has recently spread to crackles at both lung bases. Blood pressure is 176/98. A fourth heart sound (a sound in late diastole just before the first heart sound) is heard. Echocardiogram shows thick left ventricular walls with an ejection fraction of 62%. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Systolic failure from dilated cardiomyopathy
Dilated cardiomyopathy gives a weak squeeze, a reduced ejection fraction, a normal or low pressure and a third sound. Her findings are the diastolic chain.
Systolic failure from ischemic cardiomyopathy
Ischemic cardiomyopathy leads the systolic chain with a reduced ejection fraction and low-normal pressure. Her hypertension, fourth sound and preserved fraction are diastolic.
Diastolic failure from hypertrophic disease

Correct. The diastolic chain is complete: hypertension driving hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a fourth heart sound from atrial contraction against a stiff ventricle, peripheral then pulmonary edema, and a preserved ejection fraction.
High-output failure from thyroid excess
Hyperthyroid high-output failure brings tachycardia and palpitations from increased demand. Her long hypertension and fourth sound point to diastolic failure.

D.io: Stable
D.q: A 55-year-old man with stable exertional angina has a documented contraindication to beta blockers. Which medication class is used instead?
opts: Calcium channel blocker

Correct. In stable angina, a calcium channel blocker takes the place of the beta blocker when beta blockers are contraindicated, alongside lifestyle change, a statin, aspirin and sublingual nitroglycerin.
Thrombolytic agent
Thrombolytics dissolve clot in an ST-elevation infarction when percutaneous intervention is two or more hours away. They do not replace a daily anti-anginal drug.
Nonselective beta blocker
A nonselective beta blocker is still a beta blocker, so the contraindication applies. The listed alternative in stable angina is a calcium channel blocker.
Phosphodiesterase inhibitor
A phosphodiesterase inhibitor within 24 hours makes nitroglycerin contraindicated; it is not an angina drug. The replacement for a beta blocker is a calcium channel blocker.

D.io: Compare and contrast anticoagulation therapy for prosthetic heart valves.
D.q: A 60-year-old man with a mechanical aortic valve on warfarin is scheduled for a colectomy that requires stopping it. Which plan should be avoided?
opts: Rechecking his ratio after surgery
Warfarin is bridged until the international normalized ratio is therapeutic again, so rechecking it is part of the plan. What must be avoided is an unbridged gap.
Resuming a vitamin K antagonist
A mechanical valve needs lifelong vitamin K antagonist therapy, so resuming warfarin after surgery is required. The error is stopping it without a heparin bridge.
Bridging with heparin
Heparin bridging is exactly what is required when surgery interrupts warfarin in a patient with a mechanical valve. The plan to avoid is stopping warfarin with no cover.
Stopping warfarin with no bridge

Correct. If surgery requires interrupting warfarin, it must be bridged with heparin until the international normalized ratio is therapeutic; leaving a mechanical valve uncovered is the thing to avoid.

D.q: A 60-year-old hypertensive man has an electrocardiogram that does not meet voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy, but he is breathless on exertion and has a significant murmur. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Proceed to echocardiography

Correct. The voltage criteria are specific but NOT sensitive, so false negatives are common. Unexplained dyspnea and a significant murmur are both indications for echocardiography in their own right. A normal tracing does not exclude hypertrophy.
Repeat the electrocardiogram in six months
Repeating an insensitive test does not answer the question that echocardiography would.
Conclude that hypertensive heart disease is excluded
A normal electrocardiogram specifically does not exclude hypertensive heart disease, which is the practical consequence of poor sensitivity.
Order a chest radiograph to measure the cardiac size
Radiography is appropriate when pulmonary edema or cardiomegaly is suspected, but it does not assess ventricular mass, geometry or function.

D.io: Differentiate each stage of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA), natural history classification of heart failure, and associated treatment recommendations of each stage.
D.q: A 63-year-old man had a myocardial infarction a year ago. He has no symptoms of heart failure and no diabetes, and his echocardiogram shows systolic dysfunction. Which regimen is recommended?
opts: Dapagliflozin alone, since he has no symptoms
The sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor in stages A and B is for patients with diabetes, which he does not have. Stage B relies on a converting enzyme inhibitor and a beta blocker.
A converting enzyme inhibitor and a beta blocker

Correct. Asymptomatic structural disease is stage B, pre-heart failure, where an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor and a beta blocker are strong recommendations; a receptor blocker replaces the inhibitor if it is not tolerated.
Hydralazine with isosorbide dinitrate
That pairing is for symptomatic reduced ejection fraction in African American patients in functional class III or IV. Stage B relies on a converting enzyme inhibitor and a beta blocker.
A loop diuretic started at once
Diuretics are used as needed for congestion, which he does not have. Stage B relies on a converting enzyme inhibitor and a beta blocker.

D.io: Define the following diagnostic and therapeutic groups of HF patients, and the treatment implications/recommendations for each group: a. HF with reduced EF (HFrEF) b. HF with mildly reduced EF (HFmrEF) c. HF with preserved EF (HFpEF)
D.q: A 66-year-old woman with reduced ejection fraction (fraction 30%) has gained weight with leg edema and crackles. She takes a beta blocker, sacubitril-valsartan, spironolactone and dapagliflozin. Which drug relieves her fluid overload now?
opts: Diltiazem to slow the heart rate
Diltiazem is a calcium channel blocker, which is avoided in heart failure. Her congestion needs a loop diuretic.
Hydralazine given on its own
Hydralazine is paired with isosorbide dinitrate for selected patients in functional class III or IV; it does not clear fluid. Her congestion needs a loop diuretic.
A loop diuretic such as furosemide
Correct. Diuretics are used as needed for congestion in every ejection fraction group; loops such as furosemide and bumetanide are the potassium-wasting diuretics that clear fluid.
Dobutamine given at home
Dobutamine is an inotrope for intensive care use only. Her congestion needs a loop diuretic.

D.io: Non-ST segment elevation
D.q: A 64-year-old man is diagnosed with a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction. His oxygen saturation (SpO2) is 97% on room air and his heart rate is 88. Which is part of his initial treatment?
opts: Supplemental oxygen
Oxygen is given only if the oxygen saturation is below 91%. At 97% on room air, supplemental oxygen is withheld because it causes peripheral vasoconstriction.
Chewable aspirin

Correct. Unstable angina and non-ST-elevation infarction are a medical emergency treated alike: chewable aspirin, a beta blocker and intravenous nitrates if appropriate, and dual antiplatelet therapy with or without anticoagulation.
A thrombolytic agent
Thrombolytics are reserved for an ST-elevation infarction when percutaneous intervention is two or more hours away. A non-ST-elevation infarction is treated like unstable angina.
A calcium channel blocker
A beta blocker, not a calcium channel blocker, is used to reduce myocardial oxygen demand in the initial treatment. Calcium channel blockers do not improve prognosis after infarction overall.

D.io: Aortic stenosis
D.q: A 64-year-old man has an echocardiogram for palpitations that incidentally shows mild aortic stenosis. He has no chest pain, breathlessness or fainting. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: No follow-up is needed
Aortic stenosis progresses; 10 to 20% reach significant stenosis within 10 to 15 years. Evidence of it on echocardiogram calls for a cardiology consult to set follow-up.
Cardiology consultation

Correct. All patients with evidence of aortic stenosis on echocardiogram should have a cardiology consult to evaluate them and set the frequency of follow-up, even when the finding is mild and incidental.
Transcatheter valve replacement
Replacement is for severe aortic stenosis with symptomatic systolic dysfunction or a bicuspid valve. Mild asymptomatic disease is referred to cardiology for evaluation and follow-up.
Start a nitrate for prevention
Nitrates drop preload and are avoided in aortic stenosis, and medical treatment does not change its course. The step is a cardiology consult to plan follow-up.

D.io: Tricuspid stenosis
D.q: A 38-year-old woman raised in a region where rheumatic fever is common has a quivering discomfort in the neck, cold skin and right upper quadrant pain. There is a soft opening snap (a sharp sound just after the second heart sound) and a mid-diastolic rumble at the left lower sternal border near the xiphoid that grows louder with inspiration. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Mitral stenosis
Mitral stenosis is also an opening snap with a diastolic rumble, but it sits at the apex and is a left-sided murmur that does not grow with inspiration.
Pulmonic regurgitation
Pulmonic regurgitation is a brief early diastolic decrescendo at the second left intercostal space. A mid-diastolic rumble near the xiphoid is tricuspid stenosis.
Tricuspid stenosis

Correct. A rumble is stenosis and diastolic narrows it to the mitral or tricuspid valve; the left lower sternal border near the xiphoid and the inspiratory increase make it right-sided, so tricuspid stenosis. Rheumatic fever is its most common cause worldwide.
Tricuspid regurgitation
Tricuspid regurgitation is at the same location and also grows with inspiration, but it is holosystolic, not a diastolic rumble with an opening snap.

D.q: An 81-year-old woman with no history of atherosclerotic disease asks whether she should start a statin for prevention. Her low-density lipoprotein is 145 mg/dL. What is the most appropriate approach?
opts: Calculate the Pooled Cohort risk
The Pooled Cohort Equation estimates risk for ages 40 to 79, so an 81-year-old falls outside its range.
Clinical assessment and risk discussion
Correct. Above 75 in primary prevention the approach is clinical assessment and a risk discussion rather than an automatic prescription.
Automatic high-intensity statin
High intensity is not automatic above 75 in primary prevention; the decision follows assessment and discussion.
Refuse any statin due to age
Age alone does not rule out a statin; the approach is individual assessment and discussion.

D.q: A 45-year-old man has a fasting triglyceride of 780 mg/dL and low-density lipoprotein of 110 mg/dL. Diabetes, kidney disease, alcoholism and hypothyroidism have been excluded. Which management plan is most appropriate?
opts: Observation with a recheck in a year
Triglyceride above 500 carries a risk of acute pancreatitis, so it is treated now rather than watched.
Ezetimibe with a high-carbohydrate diet
Ezetimibe lowers triglyceride only 5% to 10%, and excess carbohydrate raises hepatic very-low-density triglyceride secretion.
Very low-fat diet plus a fibrate
Correct. Above 500 mg/dL the plan is a very low-fat diet (under 15% of calories from fat), weight management, physical activity and a fibrate, which lowers the pancreatitis risk.
Bile acid sequestrant with no diet change
Sequestrants lower low-density lipoprotein as adjuncts; they do not address triglyceride above 500.

D.io: Angina pectoris
D.q: A 63-year-old man describes his chest pressure while holding a clenched fist over his sternum (Levine sign). Which condition does this gesture most suggest?
opts: Myocardial ischemia
Correct. The Levine sign, a clenched fist held over the sternum while describing the discomfort, is the classic gesture of ischemic, anginal chest pain.
Pancreatitis
Pancreatic pain goes straight through to the back. A clenched fist over the sternum is the Levine sign, which points to ischemic chest pain.
Aortic dissection
Aortic dissection classically refers pain to the left or interscapular region of the back. A clenched fist over the sternum is the Levine sign of ischemic chest pain.
Biliary colic
Gallbladder pain refers to the right scapular region. The Levine sign, a fist held over the sternum, suggests myocardial ischemia instead.

D.q: A 16-year-old boy with homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia has progressive atherosclerosis despite maximal drug therapy and apheresis. Which referral may help by supplying the receptors he lacks?
opts: Bariatric surgery
Weight loss improves triglyceride and high-density lipoprotein, but cannot fix an inherited receptor defect.
Carotid ultrasound only
Imaging would describe the disease, not treat it; transplantation addresses the missing receptors.
Kidney transplantation
The kidney does not clear low-density lipoprotein through receptors; the liver is the organ that supplies them.
Liver transplantation
Correct. Liver transplantation may prove helpful in the homozygous disorder by providing low-density lipoprotein receptors that his own liver lacks or cannot use.

D.q: A 58-year-old woman has a blood pressure of 224/126 with no headache, no visual change, no chest pain, a normal neurological examination and a normal creatinine. How should this be classified?
opts: A hypertensive emergency, because the systolic exceeds 220
No absolute numeric cutoff defines an emergency; acute hypertension-mediated organ injury is what does.
Hypertensive encephalopathy
Encephalopathy would require confusion, seizures or a neurological deficit, and her examination is normal.
Severe asymptomatic hypertension

Correct. An emergency is defined by acute hypertension-mediated ORGAN INJURY, not by crossing a numeric threshold. A very high pressure with no acute organ involvement is not an emergency, and that distinction decides how fast the pressure is brought down. It is not a hypertensive emergency.
Resistant hypertension
Resistance means pressure above goal despite three complementary drugs at maximally tolerated doses, which is not what is described.

D.topic: Post-infarction care and sudden cardiac death
D.io: Acute myocardial infraction
D.q: A 70-year-old man is admitted with a large myocardial infarction and develops hypotension, cool extremities and falling urine output from cardiogenic shock. Which infarct feature makes this complication more common?
opts: A left-sided infarct

Correct. Cardiogenic shock is more common in left-sided myocardial infarctions, and left ventricular involvement carries a higher mortality. The left ventricle supplies the systemic output that shock takes away.
Reperfusion inside 90 minutes
A door-to-balloon time under 90 minutes is the goal because time is muscle; prompt reperfusion limits damage. Shock is more common with a left-sided infarct, not with timely care.
A right-sided infarct
Right ventricular infarction can tip into shock if nitroglycerin drops the preload it depends on, but as an infarct complication, cardiogenic shock is more common after left-sided infarcts.
A small subendocardial infarct
A subendocardial infarct involves only the inner wall and shows ST depression. Cardiogenic shock follows loss of pump function and is more common with left-sided infarcts.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atherosclerosis and lipid disorders: 1. Hypertriglyceridemia 2. Hypercholesterolemia 3. HDL cholesterol 4. LDL and VLDL cholesterol
D.q: A 45-year-old woman has new swelling of both legs, heavy protein in her urine and low-density lipoprotein of 220 mg/dL. Before a statin is started, which condition should be ruled out?
opts: Nephrotic syndrome
Correct. Elevated low-density lipoprotein calls for ruling out nephrotic syndrome, which drives excess very-low-density production and raises triglyceride and low-density lipoprotein.
Familial chylomicronemia
Chylomicronemia is a triglyceride disorder with pancreatitis and eruptive xanthomas, not edema and proteinuria.
Metabolic syndrome
Metabolic syndrome is diagnosed from waist, triglyceride, high-density lipoprotein, blood pressure and glucose, not proteinuria.
Heterozygous familial form
A genetic cause is sought only after secondary causes are ruled out, and her edema and proteinuria point to the kidney.
